front: Define **hardware**.
back: Hardware is the **physical components** of a computer system.

front: Name the three categories of hardware.
back: The three categories of hardware are **internal components**, **internal memory** and **hardware components**.

front: What is the role of the motherboard?
back: The motherboard **connects all the important components together**, allowing them to communicate.

front: Define **processor**.
back: A processor is an **electronic circuit that processes information**.

front:
**True or False?**

RAM and ROM are classed as internal memory.
back:
**True.**

Internal memory is one of the three categories of hardware, and it contains **RAM** and **ROM**.

front: What does a graphics card do?
back: A graphics card (**GPU**) **processes images and video**.

front: What does a sound card do?
back: A sound card **processes audio**.

front: The CPU is described as the <u>   </u> of the computer.
back: The CPU is described as the **brain** of the computer.

front: What is the purpose of an input device?
back: An input device **allows user input**, for example a mouse or a keyboard.

front: What is the purpose of an output device?
back: An output device **outputs the results of processing**, for example a monitor.

front: Define **software**.
back: Software is the set of programs that **control the hardware**; it lives on the computer system but **cannot be physically touched**.

front: What are the two categories of software?
back: The two categories of software are **application** software and **system** software.

front: Define **application software**.
back: Application software is software **chosen by a user** to help them carry out a **specific task**.

front: Define **system software**.
back: System software is software that is **essential for the operation of a computer system**.

front:
**True or False?**

Control software is system software.
back:
**False.**

Control software is **application** software, even though it controls a system.

front: What does a compiler do, and which category of software is it?
back: A compiler is **system** software that **translates high-level programming languages into machine code**.

front: What does a device driver do?
back: A device driver is **system** software that **controls hardware components and peripherals**.

front: Give three examples of application software.
back: Application software includes **word processing**, **spreadsheet**, **database management systems**, **control/measurement**, **video editing**, **graphics editing**, **audio editing** and **computer-aided design (CAD)**.

front: Define **operating system**.
back: An operating system is software that provides an **interface between the user and the hardware** in a computer system.

front: Give three things an operating system does.
back: An operating system **controls input/output devices**, **oversees the loading, running and storage of application software**, **deals with errors**, **maintains security** and **keeps a log of events**.

front: Name the four types of user interface.
back: The four types of user interface are **command line (CLI)**, **graphical (GUI)**, **dialogue-based** and **gesture-based**.

front: A command line interface uses <u>      </u> commands, whereas a graphical user interface uses visual elements.
back: A command line interface uses **text-based** commands, whereas a graphical user interface uses visual elements.

front: Define **analogue data**.
back: Analogue data is **continuous data** created from non-digital devices, which changes **gradually and smoothly**.

front: Define **digital data**.
back: Digital data is data represented in a **binary format** (1s and 0s), created and stored using digital devices.

front: Give two examples of analogue data.
back: Examples of analogue data are the **sound waves** produced when you talk, and data collected by **sensors**.

front: Give two examples of digital data.
back: Examples of digital data are **software** and **documents or files**.

front:
**True or False?**

Digital data loses quality during storage and transmission.
back:
**False.**

Digital data **maintains its quality** during storage and transmission. It is **analogue** data whose quality can be lost.

front: Define **analogue to digital conversion (ADC)**.
back: ADC is the process of taking **samples** of an analogue signal and **converting them to a binary code**.

front: Why must analogue data be converted to digital data?
back: Analogue data must be converted to digital data so that it **can be processed by a computer**.

front: Why must digital data be converted to analogue data?
back: Digital data must be converted to analogue data so that it can be **used to control devices**.

front: A higher <u>       </u> and a higher number of binary digits give a more accurate representation of the original signal.
back: A higher **sample rate** and a higher number of binary digits give a more accurate representation of the original signal.

front: What is the drawback of using a higher sample rate?
back: A higher sample rate gives a more accurate representation, but it **takes up more space** on secondary storage.

front: What is the purpose of the CPU?
back: The purpose of the CPU is to **fetch**, **decode** and **execute** instructions.

front: Define **fetch-execute cycle**.
back: The fetch-execute cycle is the cycle the CPU runs through **billions of times per second** to make a computer work.

front: Name the four key components of the CPU.
back: The four key components of the CPU are the **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)**, the **control unit (CU)**, **cache** and **registers**.

front: What happens during the fetch stage?
back: During the fetch stage the next instruction or data is **fetched from RAM** and brought back to the CPU.

front: What happens during the decode stage?
back: During the decode stage the CPU **works out what is required** from the instruction.

front: What happens during the execute stage?
back: During the execute stage the CPU **carries out the instruction** that was fetched.

front:
**True or False?**

The CPU carries out an instruction during the fetch stage.
back:
**False.**

The instruction is carried out during the **execute** stage. The fetch stage only retrieves it from RAM.

front: The three stages of the cycle are fetch, decode and <u>    </u>.
back: The three stages of the cycle are fetch, decode and **execute**.

front: Give two tasks the CPU might carry out at the execute stage.
back: At the execute stage the CPU might **perform a calculation**, **store a result back in main memory**, or **fetch data from a different location in main memory**.

front: What three things does a computer do with an input?
back: A computer **takes an input**, **processes** it and **delivers an output** for the user.

front: Define **RAM**.
back: RAM (Random Access Memory) is **primary storage** directly connected to the CPU that holds the **data and instructions currently in use**.

front: Define **ROM**.
back: ROM (Read Only Memory) is **primary storage** that holds the **first instructions a computer needs to start up**.

front:
**True or False?**

ROM is a type of secondary storage.
back:
**False.**

ROM is **primary storage**, just like RAM. Secondary storage is where data is held permanently when it is not in use.

front: Is RAM volatile or non-volatile, and what does that mean?
back: RAM is **volatile**, which means its contents are **lost when the power is turned off**.

front: Is ROM volatile or non-volatile, and what does that mean?
back: ROM is **non-volatile**, which means its contents are **not lost when the power is turned off**.

front: Can data be written to ROM?
back: No. ROM is **read only**, which means data can only be **read from** it.

front: Which is faster, RAM or ROM?
back: **RAM** is faster. ROM is fast, much faster than secondary storage, but it is **slower than RAM**.

front: Which has the larger capacity, RAM or ROM?
back: **RAM** has a much **larger capacity** than ROM.

front:
**True or False?**

ROM capacity can be increased to improve performance.
back:
**False.**

**RAM** capacity can be increased to improve performance. **ROM capacity cannot be increased.**

front: ROM contains the <u>  </u>, the Basic Input Output System.
back: ROM contains the **BIOS**, the Basic Input Output System.

front: What must happen before the CPU can use data held in secondary storage?
back: The data and instructions must be **copied from secondary storage** into RAM.

front: Where is ROM located in a computer?
back: ROM is a small **memory chip** located on the computer's **motherboard**.

front: Define **input device**.
back: An input device is a hardware component that **allows users to interact with a computer system**, entering data or commands for the computer to process.

front: Define **direct data entry device**.
back: A direct data entry device is a device capable of inputting data into a computer with **little or no human interaction**, collecting and transferring data automatically.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a keyboard.
back: A keyboard is an **easy method of entering data** and is very common, but it can cause **repetitive strain injury** and is **slow compared with direct data entry**.

front: Where is a numeric keypad commonly used?
back: A numeric keypad is commonly used in **ATMs** and **chip and PIN devices**.

front:
**True or False?**

A touchscreen is more precise than a mouse.
back:
**False.**

A touchscreen is **less precise than a mouse**, although it is intuitive and needs no separate pointing device.

front: Give two disadvantages of a microphone as an input device.
back: A microphone has **variable quality**, **verbal inputs can be inaccurate**, and the user needs to **remember key words or phrases**.

front: Why must data from an analogue sensor be converted?
back: Data from an analogue sensor **must be converted to digital data using an ADC** before a computer can process it.

front: What does OMR stand for, and what does it read?
back: OMR stands for **Optical Mark Recognition**, and it reads **marks made in pen or pencil**, for example on an exam paper.

front: What does OCR stand for, and what does it do?
back: OCR stands for **Optical Character Recognition**, and it converts **text into digital data**.

front: Which direct data entry device is used for contactless payment?
back: An **RFID reader** is used for contactless payment.

front: A <u>         </u> reader is used with debit and credit cards, but can become unreadable if damaged.
back: A **magnetic stripe** reader is used with debit and credit cards, but can become unreadable if damaged.

front: Give two advantages of a barcode reader.
back: A barcode reader is **fast and accurate**, **low cost**, allows **automatic stock control**, and is a tried and trusted technology.

front: Give two disadvantages of a barcode reader.
back: A barcode reader **requires line of sight**, barcodes are **easily damaged**, and barcodes can be **swapped or altered by consumers**.

front: What advantage does a QR code have over a barcode, and what is its main risk?
back: A QR code can **store more data than a barcode**, but QR codes can also **store malicious code**.

front: Define **output device**.
back: An output device is a hardware component that **receives information from a computer system and presents it to the user** in a comprehensible form.

front: Give two advantages of an LCD monitor.
back: An LCD monitor has **low power** consumption, is **lightweight**, has **no flickering** and suffers **no image burn-in**.

front: What advantage does an LED monitor have over an LCD monitor?
back: An LED monitor has **no motion blur or ghosting**, as well as low power consumption and a long life.

front: Give two disadvantages of a CRT monitor.
back: CRT monitors **run hot**, are **heavy** and **consume more power** than other monitor types.

front:
**True or False?**

A laser printer uses wet ink.
back:
**False.**

A laser printer uses **dry ink**. It is the **inkjet** printer that uses wet inks.

front: Give two advantages of a laser printer.
back: A laser printer is **fast**, produces **high-quality prints** and has a **lower cost per page**.

front: What is a dot matrix printer particularly good for?
back: A dot matrix printer can print **multi-part forms** and is **very good for long print runs**.

front: What is a plotter used for?
back: A plotter is used for **drawings and blueprints**, and it can print on **various materials**.

front: Give two disadvantages of a 3D printer.
back: A 3D printer has **limited materials**, is a **slow process**, is **very expensive**, and makes **counterfeit items easier to produce**.

front: Define **actuator**.
back: An actuator is an output device that **controls motors, pumps and switches**, allowing **automatic control** of many devices.

front: A multimedia projector produces a large display but requires a <u>     </u> room.
back: A multimedia projector produces a large display but requires a **darkened** room.

front: Give two disadvantages of an actuator.
back: An actuator **requires power**, is subject to **potential mechanical wear**, and **requires a DAC interface**.

front: Define **storage device**.
back: A storage device is the **hardware that reads from and writes to** storage media.

front: Define **storage media**.
back: Storage media is the **physical media that holds the non-volatile data**.

front:
**True or False?**

A storage device and storage media are two names for the same thing.
back:
**False.**

The **device** reads from and writes to the media; the **media** is what actually holds the data.

front: Name the three types of storage device.
back: The three types of storage device are **magnetic**, **solid state** and **optical**.

front: How does magnetic storage store binary data?
back: Magnetic storage uses **magnets**, specifically polarity, to store binary 0s and 1s.

front: How does solid state storage store binary data?
back: Solid state storage uses **electronic circuits** to store binary 0s and 1s.

front: How does optical storage store binary data?
back: Optical storage uses **lasers** to burn the surface of a disk, creating **pits and lands**.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of magnetic storage.
back: Magnetic storage has **high capacity** and a **low cost per gigabyte**, but it has **moving parts that can be damaged if dropped**, is **heavy and bulky**, is **prone to mechanical failure** and is **loud**.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of solid state storage.
back: Solid state storage has **very fast read/write access**, **no moving parts**, is **silent** and **portable**, but it has a **very high cost per gigabyte** and **limited read/write cycles**.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of optical storage.
back: Optical storage has a **very low cost per gigabyte**, is **small** and **silent**, but it has **very low capacity**, **very slow read/write access** and is **prone to scratches**.

front: Define **backing storage**.
back: Backing storage, also called secondary storage, is **any non-volatile storage device**, used to store data and programs when they are **not actively being used in RAM**.

front: Magnetic tape has a high capacity and low cost, but a slow access time because access is <u>      </u>.
back: Magnetic tape has a high capacity and low cost, but a slow access time because access is **sequential**.

front: Which type of storage device reads a CD, DVD or Blu-ray?
back: A CD, DVD or Blu-ray is read by an **optical** storage device.

front: Name two storage media that are read by a solid state device.
back: Solid state media include the **solid state drive (SSD)**, the **portable solid state drive**, the **USB memory stick** and **flash memory** cards such as SD or XD.

front: Define **desktop computer**.
back: A desktop computer is a computer **designed to stay in one place**, for example on a desk.

front: Define **mobile computer**.
back: A mobile computer is a computer **designed to be portable**, for example a laptop.

front: Name the three separate parts a desktop computer traditionally consists of.
back: A desktop computer traditionally consists of a separate **monitor**, **computer**, and **keyboard and mouse**.

front:
**True or False?**

Mobile computers are typically more powerful than desktop computers.
back:
**False.**

Mobile computers are typically **less powerful**, because of **power constraints due to size** and a **focus on extending battery life**.

front: Why are desktop computers easier to upgrade than mobile computers?
back: Desktop computers are **upgradable** because their parts can be replaced or changed, whereas a mobile computer's components are **integrated for size and efficiency**.

front: Give two reasons a mobile computer is less powerful than a desktop.
back: A mobile computer is less powerful because of **power constraints due to its size** and a **focus on extending battery life**.

front: Unlike a desktop computer, a mobile computer is <u>    </u> powered.
back: Unlike a desktop computer, a mobile computer is **battery** powered.

front: Give two characteristics of a smartphone.
back: A smartphone has a **small physical size**, is **easy to carry around**, has a **long battery life** and has **slower data transfer rates**.

front: How does a tablet differ from a smartphone?
back: A tablet has a **larger screen than a smartphone** and is **ideal for media consumption and web browsing**, but has **limited expandability**.

front: Give three advantages of a mobile computer.
back: Mobile computers offer **portability**, so they are easy to carry and use on the go; **flexibility**, giving access to the internet and resources from anywhere; and **multi-functionality**, so they can be used for many tasks.

front: Give three disadvantages of a mobile computer.
back: Mobile computers have **limited expandability**, are **less powerful** than desktop computers, and have a **shorter battery life** needing frequent charging.

front: Give two uses of a mobile computer for remotely controlled devices.
back: A mobile computer can be used for **controlling smart home devices**, **remote access to surveillance systems**, and **controlling drones and other devices**.

front: Define **artificial intelligence**.
back: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a machine that can **simulate intelligent behaviours similar to those of a human**.

front: Name the three things an AI system can do.
back: An AI system can **learn**, by acquiring new information; **decide**, by analysing and making choices; and **act autonomously**, by taking actions without human input.

front: Define **weak AI**.
back: Weak AI, also known as **narrow AI**, is designed to perform a **specific task or set of tasks**.

front: Define **strong AI**.
back: Strong AI, also known as **artificial general intelligence (AGI)**, is designed to perform **any intellectual task that a human can do**.

front:
**True or False?**

Narrow AI is another name for strong AI.
back:
**False.**

Narrow AI is another name for **weak** AI, which performs only a specific task. Strong AI is also known as **artificial general intelligence**.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of AI.
back: AI offers **increased efficiency**, **increased accuracy** and **scalability**, but it brings **job losses**, the **potential for biased decision making** and **ethical concerns over its use**.

front: Define **extended reality**.
back: Extended reality (XR) is an emerging technology that **blends the virtual and real worlds together** to create immersion for a user.

front: What are the two popular examples of extended reality?
back: The two popular examples of extended reality are **virtual reality (VR)** and **augmented reality (AR)**.

front: How does virtual reality work?
back: Virtual reality **shuts out the real world** and immerses the user in a **fully simulated environment**, using a headset with built-in screens giving a **360 degree view**.

front: How does augmented reality differ from virtual reality?
back: Augmented reality **overlays digital information or graphics onto the real world**, so the user is **not fully immersed** and can still see and interact with what is in front of them.

front: In virtual reality, users are often able to interact with the virtual world through <u>    </u> tracking.
back: In virtual reality, users are often able to interact with the virtual world through **motion** tracking.

front: Give two fields outside gaming where XR is applied.
back: XR is applied in **architecture**, **medicine** and **retail** for improved visualisation and interaction, and in **education and training** for a more engaging experience.

front: Define **router**.
back: A router is responsible for **routing data packets between different networks**.

front: Give three jobs a router does besides routing data packets.
back: A router **connects a LAN to the wider internet**, **manages and prioritises data traffic** to keep connections stable, and **assigns IP addresses** to devices on the network.

front: Define **data packet**.
back: A data packet is a small **chunk of data** that makes up a larger piece of data which has been **broken down so that it can be transmitted** over the internet.

front: Name the three parts of a data packet.
back: A data packet consists of a **header**, a **payload** and a **trailer**.

front: What does the header of a data packet contain?
back: The header contains the **source IP address**, the **destination IP address**, the **packet number** and **error checking** such as checksums.

front: What is a network interface card required for?
back: A network interface card (**NIC**) is **required for a computer to connect to a network**, and it can be **wired or wireless**.

front: Define **hub**.
back: A hub is a networking device used to **connect multiple devices** in a network. It is a **'dumb' device** that passes on anything received on one connection to **all other connections**.

front:
**True or False?**

A switch sends data to every device on the network.
back:
**False.**

A **hub** sends all data to all devices. A **switch** only sends data to the device it was intended for, which improves network efficiency.

front: Define **MAC address**.
back: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a **unique identifier given to devices which communicate over a local area network**, assigned to the NIC during manufacturing.

front: How does a switch know where to send a data packet?
back: A switch examines the packet's **destination MAC address** and looks that address up in its **lookup table**, then forwards the packet to the corresponding device.

front: Define **bridge**.
back: A bridge is a device used to **connect two local area networks together** to create one larger network.

front: How does a bridge differ from a switch or a hub?
back: Unlike a switch or hub, a bridge **only connects local area networks together**.

front:
**True or False?**

A device's MAC address changes when it joins a different network.
back:
**False.**

MAC addresses are **static** and never change. It is the **IP address** that is dynamic and changes when a device moves to a different network.

front: A MAC address is made up of 12 <u>           </u>   digits, usually grouped in pairs.
back: A MAC address is made up of 12 **hexadecimal** digits, usually grouped in pairs.

front: Define **wireless network**.
back: A wireless network is a network where connections are made **using radio waves to transmit data through the air**.

front: Name the two most common types of wireless connection.
back: The two most common types of wireless connection are **Wi-Fi** and **Bluetooth**.

front: What does a device communicate with when using Wi-Fi?
back: A device communicates with a **hotspot** or a **wireless access point (WAP)**, which can be a standalone device or built into a **router or switch**.

front: Give three situations where Wi-Fi is preferred over Bluetooth.
back: Wi-Fi is preferred when **high speed data transfer is required**, when **long range communication is required**, and when **many devices need to be connected at the same time**.

front: Give two advantages of Wi-Fi.
back: Wi-Fi offers **portability**, since location is only limited by range; **lower cost** to set up and add new devices; and **compatibility**, as most devices have a built-in Wi-Fi adapter.

front: Give two disadvantages of Wi-Fi.
back: Wi-Fi has **slower data transfer than Ethernet**, is **less secure than Ethernet**, and its **range relies on signal strength** to the WAP, so signals can be obstructed.

front: What is Bluetooth typically used for?
back: Bluetooth is typically used for a **direct connection between two devices**, such as headphones, controllers, keyboards and mice.

front: What happens when two Bluetooth devices pair?
back: They **exchange a cryptographic key**, which is used to generate a **secret shared key**. This **encrypts the data** between them and creates a **Wireless Personal Area Network (WPAN)**.

front: Define **frequency hopping spread spectrum (FHSS)**.
back: FHSS is where connected devices **continuously change their transmitting frequency between 79 different channels** to avoid interference and improve the reliability of the connection.

front:
**True or False?**

Bluetooth has a longer range than Wi-Fi.
back:
**False.**

Bluetooth has a maximum range of about **30 metres**, whereas Wi-Fi reaches about **100 metres**, depending on obstructions.

front: How many connections can Bluetooth support compared with Wi-Fi?
back: Bluetooth supports a maximum of **7** connections, whereas Wi-Fi supports a maximum of **30**.

front: Bluetooth has very low <u>   </u> consumption, which makes it ideal for personal devices.
back: Bluetooth has very low **power** consumption, which makes it ideal for personal devices.

front: Define **cloud storage**.
back: Cloud storage is **long-term secondary storage of data that resides in a remote location**, accessible only via a **wide area network** such as the internet.

front: Where is cloud data physically stored?
back: Cloud data is stored on **remote servers**, typically using magnetic storage (**HDD**), but increasingly using solid state (**SSD**).

front: Name the three types of cloud storage.
back: The three types of cloud storage are **public cloud**, **private cloud** and **hybrid cloud**.

front: Define **public cloud**.
back: In a public cloud, the customer and the cloud storage provider are **different companies**.

front: Define **private cloud**.
back: In a private cloud, the customer and the cloud storage provider are a **single organisation**.

front: Define **hybrid cloud**.
back: A hybrid cloud **combines public and private cloud options**, allowing **sensitive data to remain private** while providing public cloud services for less sensitive information.

front:
**True or False?**

Cloud storage can be used without an internet connection.
back:
**False.**

A **stable internet connection is required** to use cloud storage.

front: Give three advantages of cloud storage.
back: Data can be **accessed from anywhere** and **on any device**; it can be **shared quickly** with anyone holding the relevant permissions; capacity can be **increased or decreased as needed**; providers use **multiple servers to back up data**; providers offer **advanced security features**; and there is **no need to hire specialist staff**.

front: Give three disadvantages of cloud storage.
back: A **stable internet connection is required**; data may be **vulnerable to security breaches**; the user is **dependent on the provider** for availability and reliability; **data may be lost** if the company ceases to exist; and the service can become **expensive over time**.

front: What is the difference between cloud storage and local storage?
back: Cloud storage involves storing data on **remote servers accessed via the internet**, while local storage refers to storing data on **physical devices** such as hard drives or flash drives.

front: Cloud providers protect user data with security features such as data <u>  </u> and multi-factor authentication.
back: Cloud providers protect user data with security features such as data **encryption** and multi-factor authentication.

front: How do cloud providers reduce the risk of data loss from hardware failure?
back: Providers often use **multiple servers** to store and **back up data**, reducing the risk of data loss due to hardware failure.

front: Define **the internet**.
back: The internet is a **global network of networks**: multiple local area networks connected together to form a large wide area network.

front:
**True or False?**

The World Wide Web and the internet are the same thing.
back:
**False.**

The web is a **collection of websites and web pages accessed using** the internet. The **internet** is the underlying network that provides the connectivity.

front: Once authenticated, what level of access does an extranet user get?
back: Once authenticated, an extranet user has **managed access** to network resources and information.

front: Which type of network is the internet an example of?
back: The internet is the most well-known **wide area network (WAN)**.

front: How are web pages accessed?
back: Web pages are accessed using a **web browser**, which communicates with **web servers** to retrieve and display the content.

front: Define **intranet**.
back: An intranet is a **private** network designed to work much like the internet, but which **operates only within a local area network**.

front: Who can access an intranet, and what keeps it secure?
back: An intranet can be accessed **only by authorised users**, exclusively the organisation's **employees**. It sits **behind a firewall** to ensure security.

front: Give two advantages of an intranet over the internet.
back: An intranet offers **better bandwidth**, keeps **data within the organisation**, carries **less chance of hacking and attacks**, and lets administrators **manage access to external sites and links**.

front: Define **extranet**.
back: An extranet is an **extension to an intranet** that allows **authorised access from outside** the local area network.

front: Who is an extranet useful for providing access to?
back: An extranet is useful for providing access to **customers**, **clients** and **key stakeholders**.

front: Give two similarities between the internet, an intranet and an extranet.
back: They are all **web based technologies**, they all allow users to **access information remotely**, they all use **client server architecture**, they all use security measures such as **authentication and encryption**, and they all **facilitate information and resource sharing**.

front: An intranet is accessible to employees of the organisation and not to members of the <u>     </u> .
back: An intranet is accessible to employees of the organisation and not to members of the **public**.

front: Define **network**.
back: A network is **two or more devices connected together** with the purpose of **sharing resources**.

front: Define **local area network (LAN)**.
back: A LAN is a network with a **small geographical area**, under one mile, in which **all of the hardware is owned by the company, organisation or household using it**.

front: Define **wide area network (WAN)**.
back: A WAN is a network with a **large geographical area**, over one mile, made up of a **collection of LANs joined together**.

front: Define **wireless local area network (WLAN)**.
back: A WLAN is a local area network where devices connect to the network **wirelessly instead of using cables**.

front: What extra hardware does a WLAN need?
back: A WLAN needs **wireless access points (WAPs)** or **hotspots** connected to the network so that users can connect using Wi-Fi.

front:
**True or False?**

All the hardware in a WAN is owned by the organisation using it.
back:
**False.**

In a **LAN** all the hardware is owned by the organisation using it. In a **WAN** the hardware is **not all owned** by them, for example telephone lines owned by telecommunication companies.

front: The computers on a wide area network are connected via <u>    </u>.
back: The computers on a wide area network are connected via **routers**.

front: What types of connection does a LAN use?
back: A LAN uses **unshielded twisted pair (UTP) cable**, **fibre optic cable** or **wireless connections (Wi-Fi)**.

front: Give two advantages of a LAN.
back: A LAN allows **centralised management** of updates, backups and software installations; lets devices be **secured** with firewalls and antivirus software; allows users to **share resources** such as printers; and allows users to **collaborate and share files and folders**.

front: Give two disadvantages of a LAN.
back: If **hardware fails** the network may not function properly; networks are **more prone to attacks** than standalone computers; access can be **slow depending on network traffic**; and they **require costly maintenance**.

front: Give two disadvantages of a WLAN.
back: A WLAN has **limited coverage**, which walls and other structures can worsen; **bandwidth speeds** can suffer in high traffic areas; there can be **interference from other devices**; and it is **vulnerable to security threats** because wireless signals can be intercepted.

front: What types of connection does a WAN use to join LANs together?
back: A WAN uses **fibre optic cable**, **telephone lines** and **satellite** to connect the LANs together.

front: Why does transferring data across a network pose a security risk?
back: Transferring data poses potential security risks of **unauthorised access** and **data manipulation**.

front: How do hackers create a data transfer risk?
back: Hackers **exploit network weaknesses** and then **access, delete or steal confidential data**.

front: Define **insider threat**.
back: An insider threat is someone **intentionally or unintentionally compromising network security policies**, leading to data interception or theft.

front: How does social engineering create a data transfer risk?
back: Social engineering **manipulates network users into giving away confidential information** or clicking links which install malware, leading to the compromise of data.

front:
**True or False?**

Using HTTP rather than HTTPS for sensitive information is an insecure protocol risk.
back:
**True.**

Using **HTTP instead of HTTPS** when dealing with sensitive information is an **insecure protocol** risk.

front: Give the two encryption-related causes of data transfer risk.
back: **Unencrypted transfers**, where no encryption protocols are used for sensitive data, and **weak encryption**, where weak or outdated encryption protocols are used.

front: Define **password**.
back: A password is a **digital lock to prevent unauthorised access to an account**.

front: How are passwords stored in a database, and why?
back: Passwords are stored as an **encrypted or ciphered text entry**, so that even with unauthorised access to the database a hacker **would not be able to gain access to the individual passwords**.

front: Give the four features of a strong password.
back: A strong password has a **mixture of upper and lower case**, contains **at least one number**, contains **at least one symbol**, and is a **minimum of eight characters**.

front: A strong password should be a minimum of <u>   </u> characters long.
back: A strong password should be a minimum of **eight** characters long.

front: Why should anti-spyware software be used to help keep passwords safe?
back: Anti-spyware software is used to ensure that **keyloggers are not used** to capture passwords.

front: Why should passwords be changed periodically?
back: Passwords should be changed periodically to ensure they **have not been compromised**.

front: Define **authentication**.
back: Authentication is the process of **ensuring that a system is secure** by asking the user to **complete tasks to prove they are an authorised user** of the system.

front: Why is authentication needed?
back: Authentication is needed because **bots can submit data in online forms**.

front: Name the four authentication methods.
back: The four methods are **zero login and biometrics**, **magnetic stripe**, **smart cards**, and **physical and electronic tokens**.

front: Define **zero login**.
back: Zero login allows a user to **log in without using a username and password**, using **biometric data** to create a profile so they do not have to authenticate each time.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of zero login and biometrics.
back: It is **convenient** for devices where users log in frequently, but if **compromised, biometric data cannot be changed**, and recognition can be **less than perfect**, leading to failed logins.

front: How does a magnetic stripe card authenticate a user?
back: The magnetic stripe **contains unique data** such as ID, name and date of birth. When **swiped through a magnetic card reader**, those details are used to identify the user.

front: Give two advantages of magnetic stripe cards.
back: They are **easy and cheap to set up**, can be used to **access multiple systems**, and can be **remotely deactivated**.

front: How does a smart card improve on a magnetic stripe card?
back: A smart card adds a **microchip** to create a **contactless card**. The microchip **stores additional information** such as a PIN for an extra layer of security, and the **data is encrypted**.

front:
**True or False?**

Smart cards are less secure than magnetic stripe cards.
back:
**False.**

Smart cards are **more secure** than magnetic stripe cards, because the data is encrypted and the microchip can store a PIN.

front: Define **physical token**.
back: A physical token is a **physical device used to authenticate a user remotely**, which **generates a random one time password (OTP)** that the user must type in.

front: How does an electronic token differ from a physical token?
back: An electronic token is a **software token generated by an app**. The user authenticates in the app, for example with a fingerprint, and an OTP is generated. It is **more convenient** than carrying a physical device.

front: One time passwords generated by a physical token <u>    </u> after a few minutes.
back: One time passwords generated by a physical token **change** after a few minutes.

front: Define **anti-malware software**.
back: Anti-malware software is a **combination of different software** used to prevent computers from being susceptible to **viruses and other malicious software**.

front: Name the three types of software that anti-malware includes.
back: Anti-malware includes **anti-virus**, **anti-spam** and **anti-spyware**.

front: What does anti-malware software scan?
back: Anti-malware scans through **email attachments**, **websites** and **downloaded files** to search for threats.

front: What is a malware signature used for?
back: Anti-malware holds a list of **known malware signatures** so that it can **block them immediately** if they try to access the device in any way.

front: Why does anti-malware software check for updates?
back: It checks for updates to ensure its **database of known issues is up to date**.

front: Define **quarantine** in the context of anti-malware.
back: Quarantining is **isolating infected files**, which allows threats to be **automatically deleted** and lets the user decide whether the file is a genuine threat.

front: Define **heuristic checking**.
back: Heuristic checking is the identification of potential threats within a file from **behavioural patterns and characteristics**.

front:
**True or False?**

Heuristic checking relies only on a database of known viruses.
back:
**False.**

Heuristic checking identifies threats from **behavioural patterns and characteristics**, rather than relying only on a database of known viruses.

front: Anti-malware software will scan <u>  </u> storage media when it is connected to the device.
back: Anti-malware software will scan **external** storage media when it is connected to the device.

front: Why is quarantining a file better than deleting it immediately?
back: Quarantining allows the user to **determine if the file is a legitimate threat and not a false positive**.

front: Define **video-conferencing**.
back: Video-conferencing is a way of enabling **real-time audio and visual communication between geographically separated parties**.

front: What hardware is required to host a video-conference?
back: A video-conference requires a **webcam**, a **large output display** such as a projector, screen or TV, a **microphone** and **speakers**.

front: What specialist software is required for video-conferencing?
back: Video-conferencing requires **drivers** to control the output of the webcam and a **codec** to encode and decode the data being transmitted.

front: Define **codec**.
back: A codec is software that **encodes (compresses) and decodes (decompresses)** data being transmitted.

front: Give three advantages of video-conferencing.
back: It offers **convenience** and **cost saving**, is **better for the environment**, means **attendees do not have to travel**, lets **anyone within the company attend regardless of location**, allows events **at short notice**, and some software allows **record and playback**.

front: Give three disadvantages of video-conferencing.
back: The **initial equipment purchase can be costly**, there are **time zone issues** across locations, users **may need training**, it requires a **strong and stable network connection**, **picture and sound quality can be poor**, and **delays can disrupt the flow** of the meeting.

front: Define **audio-conferencing**.
back: Audio-conferencing is a way of enabling real-time **audio only** communication between geographically separated parties, using standard **phone lines**.

front: How is an audio-conference set up and joined?
back: The phone company gives the host a **personal PIN** and a **participant PIN**. The host starts the conference with their **personal PIN**, and participants **dial in** using the **participant PIN**.

front: What can be used on computers to hold audio-conferences?
back: **Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP)** can be used on computers to hold audio-conferences.

front: Give two advantages of audio-conferencing.
back: It is **cheaper than video-conferencing** because less hardware is required, is **more accessible** because less training is needed, and lets participants **focus only on voice** without visual distraction.

front: Give two disadvantages of audio-conferencing.
back: Participants can **lose focus** through lack of visual interaction, a **lack of visual clues may lead to miscommunication**, **audio quality can be poor**, and it **does not suit collaboration**.

front: Define **web-conferencing**.
back: Web-conferencing is a way of enabling real-time audio and visual communication between geographically separated parties **on the internet**.

front:
**True or False?**

Web-conferencing is ideal for small groups of users.
back:
**False.**

**Video**-conferencing is ideal for **small groups**. **Web**-conferencing is ideal for **large groups**, and is typically used for webinars, lectures and presentations.

front: What is the key difference between web-conferencing and video-conferencing?
back: Video-conferencing focuses on **face to face communication**, whereas web-conferencing focuses on **interaction and collaboration**, such as document sharing and virtual whiteboards.

front: To host a web-conference, the emphasis is placed on a high-speed, stable <u>  </u> connection.
back: To host a web-conference, the emphasis is placed on a high-speed, stable **internet** connection.

front: Define **microprocessor**.
back: A microprocessor is an **integrated circuit that contains a central processing unit**, and it is responsible for **executing instructions**.

front: Give three devices in the home that microprocessors monitor and control.
back: Microprocessors in the home monitor and control **central heating systems**, **security alarm systems** and **home entertainment systems**.

front: Name the three areas of life affected by microprocessor-controlled devices in the home.
back: They affect **lifestyle**, **leisure** and **physical fitness**.

front: Give two positive effects of microprocessor-controlled devices on lifestyle.
back: They mean **fewer manual tasks**, devices can be **controlled from outside the home**, and **live security alerts** can be sent straight to a smartphone or computer.

front:
**True or False?**

Microprocessor-controlled devices only have positive effects on physical fitness.
back:
**False.**

They can cause a **loss of fitness** through fewer manual tasks, make people **lazy** through dependence on devices, create **unrealistic expectations** by comparing progress with others, and **biometric data is not always accurate**.

front: Give two negative effects of smart devices on social interaction.
back: They can lead to **social isolation**, **increased anxiety** from a lack of interaction, and differences in **the way people behave online compared to offline**.

front: Why does any device fitted with a microprocessor create a security risk?
back: Any device fitted with a microprocessor is **open to cybercriminal activity**, giving hackers more opportunities, for example **hacking smart home cameras and locks**, or **monitoring smart heating patterns** to work out when people are at home.

front: Give four transport systems that microprocessors monitor and control.
back: Microprocessors are used in **traffic management** such as smart motorways, **ANPR**, **air traffic control in airports** and **railway signalling**.

front: Give two advantages of monitoring and controlling transport with microprocessors.
back: There is **less human error**, reducing accidents; **efficient scheduling** means more trains or aeroplanes can run; **ANPR** can automatically penalise offences and check insurance; and **smart motorways** adapt in real time to reduce journey times.

front: Give two disadvantages of monitoring and controlling transport with microprocessors.
back: If the **system fails the whole transport system stops**, it is **open to attack by cybercriminals**, **ANPR raises privacy concerns** by collecting data, and **design flaws can lead to safety concerns**.

front: Autonomous vehicles use sensors, cameras, actuators and microprocessors to travel without <u>   </u> intervention.
back: Autonomous vehicles use sensors, cameras, actuators and microprocessors to travel without **human** intervention.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of autonomous vehicles.
back: They are **better for the environment** through efficiency, **safer** with no human error, and **reduce traffic congestion**. However they are **expensive**, raise **security concerns** around software updates, need **higher maintenance**, could cause **unemployment**, and face **user reluctance**.

front: Name the four health issues caused by prolonged use of IT.
back: The four health issues are **repetitive strain injury (RSI)**, **back and neck problems**, **eye strain** and **headaches**.

front: Define **repetitive strain injury**.
back: Repetitive strain injury is **damage to the fingers, wrists and joints**, traditionally caused by **prolonged use of a keyboard and mouse**.

front: Give three effects of repetitive strain injury.
back: The effects of RSI are **pain**, **numbness**, **weakness** and **stiffness**.

front: Give three ways to reduce the risk of repetitive strain injury.
back: Have the **correct posture**, use a **wrist support** if necessary, **take regular breaks**, and use an **ergonomic keyboard**.

front: What causes back and neck problems when using IT?
back: Back and neck problems are caused by **sitting in front of a computer screen for prolonged periods of time**.

front: Give three ways to reduce the risk of back and neck problems.
back: Use an **adjustable chair**, take **regular breaks**, and use a **foot rest**.

front: What causes eye strain?
back: Eye strain is caused by **staring at a computer screen for prolonged periods of time**, or by **incorrect lighting causing reflections**.

front: Give three effects of eye strain.
back: The effects of eye strain are **headaches**, **vision problems** such as blurred or double vision and light sensitivity, and general **discomfort**.

front: Give three ways to reduce the risk of eye strain.
back: **Take regular breaks**, use an **anti-glare screen filter**, and **change from a CRT to an LCD monitor**.

front:
**True or False?**

Headaches when using IT are caused by a single factor.
back:
**False.**

Headaches are caused by a **combination of factors**, including **poor lighting**, **flickering screens**, **reflections** and **fatigue**.

front: To reduce the risk of headaches a user should take regular breaks, use an anti-glare screen filter and have regular <u>  </u> tests.
back: To reduce the risk of headaches a user should take regular breaks, use an anti-glare screen filter and have regular **eye** tests.

front: Which single prevention strategy applies to all four health issues?
back: **Taking regular breaks** is recommended for RSI, back and neck problems, eye strain and headaches.

front: Define **communication media**.
back: Communication media describes the **tools and channels for sharing information between a sender and a receiver**, and can be both electronic and physical.

front: Define **newsletter**.
back: A newsletter is a **periodic publication** used to inform, educate or entertain subscribers about specific topics, usually distributed by email or as printed copies.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of newsletters.
back: Newsletters are **cost effective**, give **measurable results**, are **easy to personalise** and **targeted**. However they suffer **low engagement**, can be blocked by **spam filters**, offer **limited interactivity** and can **get lost in a busy inbox**.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of posters.
back: Posters are **cost effective**, have **wide reach**, are **versatile** and have a **long shelf life** in the right space. However they carry **limited information**, **lack interactivity**, can be **removed or defaced**, and **cannot be updated**.

front: Give three disadvantages of using a website as communication media.
back: A website **can be hacked**, carries a **risk of pharming**, and its **maintenance can be expensive**.

front: Give three disadvantages of multimedia presentations.
back: They require **special equipment**, often require **internet access**, it is **easy to create a bad presentation**, and **visuals can take focus from the overall message**.

front: Define **media streaming**.
back: Media streaming is the **real-time transmission of audio and video files over the internet**, allowing users to access content **without downloading it** to their devices.

front: Define **e-publication**.
back: An e-publication is a **digital version of printed material**, such as an eBook, eMagazine or eNewspaper.

front: Give three benefits of e-publications.
back: E-publications offer **portability**, **searchability** and **adjustable text size**.

front: Define **mobile communication**.
back: Mobile communication involves **transmitting information between people and devices using radio waves**.

front: What does a SIM card do?
back: A subscriber identity module (SIM) card **links the device to a network carrier**, allowing it to make phone calls and send messages.

front:
**True or False?**

Voice over internet protocol requires cellular reception.
back:
**False.**

VoIP provides audio and visual communication **via the internet** and requires extra apps installed on the device. It is ordinary **phone calls** that require cellular reception.

front: SMS messages are stored on the device and use virtual keyboards and <u>  </u> text.
back: SMS messages are stored on the device and use virtual keyboards and **predictive** text.

front: Give two uses of a smartphone camera besides taking photographs.
back: The camera is used for **video calls** and can act as a **barcode scanner for QR codes**.

front: Define **computer modelling**.
back: Computer modelling is **using a computer to simulate a real-life system** in order to study its behaviour in different scenarios.

front: What is the purpose of running a simulation on a model?
back: The simulation uses a model to help **predict how the system will work in unusual circumstances**.

front: Name five applications of computer modelling.
back: Computer modelling is applied to **personal finance**, **bridge and building design**, **flood water management**, **traffic management** and **weather forecasting**.

front: Give three advantages of computer modelling.
back: It is **cheaper** than building the real thing, makes it **easier to try a range of scenarios**, is **safer** because hazardous environments can be simulated, is **faster** because variables can be sped up, and allows **testing before real-life construction begins**.

front:
**True or False?**

A well-designed computer model can be 100% accurate.
back:
**False.**

A computer model will **never be 100% accurate**. Results are only as good as the **model designed and the data entered**.

front: Give three disadvantages of computer modelling.
back: A model will **never be 100% accurate**, **results are only as good as the model and the data entered**, and **human error in the design could skew results**.

front: How is computer modelling used in personal finance?
back: A **spreadsheet** is used to test **'what if' scenarios**, changing values to see the impact, for example the financial effect on a family if household income went down.

front: Give three things a model can test in bridge design.
back: A bridge model can test **how much traffic the bridge can take**, the **effects of natural vibrations**, the **effects of different weather conditions**, and the **impact of an accident on structural integrity**.

front: Give two things a model can test in building design.
back: A building model can test the **effects of different weather conditions**, **simulate fire evacuation protocols**, and assess the **impact of a fire on structural integrity**.

front: What does an automated flood defence system allow?
back: It allows **real-time monitoring**, **data collection**, and a **faster response to changing conditions**, such as advance warning to people.

front: In traffic management, the data collected can be used to optimise the <u>        </u> times at different junctions.
back: In traffic management, the data collected can be used to optimise the **traffic light** times at different junctions.

front: What data do sensors collect for weather forecasting, and how is the model checked?
back: Sensors collect **air pressure**, **wind speed**, **air temperature** and **humidity**. The **actual weather is compared to the modelled data** to check accuracy and identify areas of the model to modify.

front: Define **computer controlled system**.
back: A computer controlled system uses **computers and software to control, monitor and manage** processes, machines or devices.

front: What does the effectiveness of a computer controlled system depend on?
back: Its effectiveness depends on the quality of the **software**, the **hardware** and the **input data**.

front: Give three advantages of computer controlled systems.
back: They give **increased efficiency and productivity** by working 24/7, **greater precision and accuracy**, the **ability to operate in hazardous environments**, **reduced human error and fatigue**, and can **work with large or delicate items**.

front: Give three disadvantages of computer controlled systems.
back: They have **high initial investment and maintenance costs**, cause **job displacement for human workers**, create **dependency on reliable software and hardware**, **lack flexibility for unexpected situations**, and **require costly backup systems**.

front: Define **robotics**.
back: Robotics is the principle of a robot **carrying out a task by following a precise set of programmed instructions**.

front: What are the two groups of robots?
back: Robots are categorised as **dumb robots** and **smart robots**.

front:
**True or False?**

A dumb robot can adapt and learn.
back:
**False.**

A **dumb** robot repeats the same programmed instructions over and over, with **no AI**. A **smart** robot uses **AI** to carry out more complex tasks and can **adapt and learn**.

front: Give an example of a dumb robot and a smart robot.
back: A dumb robot example is a **car assembly line**. A smart robot example is **assisting surgeons in delicate procedures**.

front: Name the four ethical and legal issues raised by AI and robotics.
back: The four issues are **accountability**, **safety**, **algorithmic bias** and **legal liability**.

front: What is the role of a robot in industry, and one drawback?
back: In industry a robot acts as a **quality inspector**, using **advanced vision to inspect products for defects**. However it **may not work on defects that require human judgement**.

front: What is the role of a robot in agriculture, and one drawback?
back: In agriculture a robot acts as a **planting and seeding machine**, giving **precise planting** at optimum depths and distances. However there are **high upfront costs** and it may **struggle with uneven terrain and changing weather**.

front: What is the role of a robot in medicine, and its key limitation?
back: In medicine a robot acts as a **rehabilitation therapist**, giving **personalised physical therapy exercises** to aid recovery. Its key limitation is that it **does not provide emotional support**.

front: Warehouse robots bring efficiency, but create high <u>        </u> costs and safety concerns for human workers sharing the space.
back: Warehouse robots bring efficiency, but create high **infrastructure** costs and safety concerns for human workers sharing the space.

front: Give one drawback of an educational robot used in entertainment.
back: Educational robots have a **high cost** and **cannot replace the guidance of human teachers**.

front: Define **school management system**.
back: A school management system is a **software solution designed to centralise and streamline a school's administrative tasks**, with **data stored centrally** to improve efficiency.

front: Name the three processes a school management system can include.
back: It can include **registration and attendance**, **recording learner performance**, and **computer aided learning (CAL)**.

front: Give three advantages of a school management system.
back: It gives **streamlined administration and record-keeping**, **improved communication** between teachers, students and parents, **centralised access to information**, **data-driven decision-making**, **more up to date information**, and information that can be **obtained quickly in an emergency**.

front: Give three disadvantages of a school management system.
back: The **cost**, a **time consuming and complex transition**, the **training required**, **dependence on technology**, and **data security concerns**.

front: Besides a teacher entering data manually, how can attendance be recorded?
back: IT systems make other methods possible, such as **magnetic stripe cards** and **biometrics**.

front: How does a school management system help tackle truancy?
back: **Patterns of absence can be found quickly**, which helps to tackle truancy and lateness, and letters or texts can be **automatically sent to parents**.

front: Give three uses of the data collected on learner performance.
back: The data can be used to **identify class and individual strengths and areas for development**, to **inform teaching strategies**, to **provide individual progress reports**, and to **critically analyse class and teacher performance**.

front: Define **computer aided learning (CAL)**.
back: Computer aided learning allows students to **work on individual development areas**.

front:
**True or False?**

Computer aided learning is designed to replace traditional classroom teaching.
back:
**False.**

CAL is designed to **enhance and not replace** traditional classroom teaching.

front: What can computer aided learning provide to aid exam performance?
back: CAL can provide **interactive revision resources** to aid exam performance.

front: If a student arrives after a certain time, their attendance record is <u>    </u> as late or absent.
back: If a student arrives after a certain time, their attendance record is **flagged** as late or absent.

front: Why is a school management system valuable in a fire or emergency?
back: Information about a student can be **obtained quickly** in an emergency, because the system holds **accurate and up to date records**.

front: Define **online booking system**.
back: An online booking system is a computer system that **allows customers to purchase tickets for events online**.

front: Name four industries that use online booking systems.
back: **Travel**, for flights, hotels and package holidays; **music**, for live event tickets; **film**, for cinema tickets with seat selection; and **sport**, for event tickets with a chosen view.

front: Give three advantages of an online booking system for the customer.
back: **Convenience and accessibility** with 24/7 booking, **instant confirmation and ticketing**, the ability to **compare prices and options**, **promotions and personalised offers**, being **faster to change or cancel**, and **automated reminders** by email or text.

front: Give two advantages of an online booking system for the business.
back: **Repeated bookings can easily be made**, and **staff are freed up to do other things**.

front: Give three disadvantages of online booking systems.
back: The potential for **technical issues and downtime**, possible **security and privacy concerns**, **transaction and booking fees**, **impersonal customer service**, the need for an **internet connected device**, and **staff may lose their job**.

front:
**True or False?**

Seats stay available to other customers while one customer is paying.
back:
**False.**

Once a seat is selected it is **temporarily made unavailable for booking by any other user** while the customer completes payment.

front: What happens after the customer chooses a film and a date?
back: The **database is searched** and the **times and availability are displayed** on the screen.

front: What is displayed once a customer chooses a suitable time?
back: The **screen seating chart** is displayed, showing which seats are **available and taken**.

front: What is sent to the customer once payment is taken?
back: A **confirmation message** is displayed, and a **payment receipt and QR code e-ticket** are emailed.

front: What is the final step of the booking process?
back: The **database is updated to make the seats unavailable**.

front: If no seats are available, the system outputs an <u>   </u> message.
back: If no seats are available, the system outputs an **error** message.

front: What happens to the number of seats available once a booking is confirmed?
back: The system **reduces the number of seats or tickets available by the number booked**, and **flags the seat as booked**.

front: Define **ATM**.
back: An Automatic Teller Machine is used in the banking industry to provide customers with **convenient access to financial transactions 24/7**.

front: Give four things a customer can do at an ATM.
back: A customer can **withdraw cash**, **deposit cash or cheques**, **check their account balance**, obtain a **mini statement**, **pay bills**, and make **money transfers**.

front: Give three advantages of ATMs.
back: ATMs give **convenient access to banking services**, are **available 24/7**, offer **reduced waiting time**, and provide **global access to funds**.

front: Give three disadvantages of ATMs.
back: ATMs have **cash withdrawal limits**, carry a **risk of theft or fraud**, offer **limited services compared to a bank branch**, suffer **technical issues and downtime**, and **some banks charge** for using them.

front: Define **EFT**.
back: Electronic Funds Transfer is a way of **moving money from one account to another**.

front: What is EFT primarily used for?
back: EFT is used primarily for **salary deposits**, **bill payments** and **online purchases**.

front: Define **EFTPOS**.
back: Electronic Funds Transfer at the Point of Sale is used by retailers to **allow customers to make purchases using debit or credit cards**.

front: Describe the first three steps of an EFTPOS transaction.
back: **Data is read from the chip**, using RFID or NFC if the payment is contactless; the **business bank's computer contacts the customer's bank's computer**; and the **card is checked to see if it is valid**.

front: What happens once the card is found to be valid in an EFTPOS transaction?
back: The transaction continues, an **authorisation code is sent to the business**, the **price is deducted from the customer's account**, and that money is **added to the business's account**.

front:
**True or False?**

EFT transactions can be disputed for up to 60 days.
back:
**True.**

Being able to **dispute a transaction for up to 60 days** is an advantage of EFT.

front: Give three disadvantages of EFT.
back: EFT carries a **risk of online fraud**, suffers **technical issues**, **requires an internet connection**, and **requires immediate funds to be available**.

front: Define **internet banking**.
back: Internet banking is a **secure online platform for accessing and controlling a person's bank account**, used through a secure website or the bank's official app.

front: Give three advantages of internet banking.
back: Internet banking offers **convenience and 24/7 access**, **easy account management**, a **reduced need for branch visits**, potentially **better interest rates**, and makes it **easier to shop around for the best account**.

front: A key disadvantage of internet banking is that physical <u>  </u> cannot be deposited or withdrawn.
back: A key disadvantage of internet banking is that physical **cash** cannot be deposited or withdrawn.

front: Define **information system**.
back: An information system is a purpose built system designed to **collect, store, process, distribute and use information**.

front: Give four uses of an information system in a hospital.
back: A hospital information system is used to **access patient medical records**, handle **appointment scheduling**, **manage medication dispensing**, **facilitate communication between healthcare providers**, and support **public health reporting**.

front: Why do healthcare professionals use information systems?
back: They use them for making **informed decisions about patient care**.

front: Define **3D printer**.
back: A 3D printer is a machine capable of **outputting three-dimensional objects from a digital file**.

front: How does the 3D printing process start?
back: 3D printing starts with the **creation of a 3D model using computer aided design (CAD)**.

front: Give the two general benefits of 3D printing.
back: 3D models can be **fully customised on the computer before printing**, and 3D printing supports **prototyping**.

front: How are 3D printers used for prosthetics?
back: They produce **custom-made prosthetic limbs or body parts** tailored to a patient's specific needs, **faster and more affordably** than traditional methods.

front: Define **tissue engineering**.
back: Tissue engineering is the **3D printing of living cells to create functional tissues**, which can be used to repair or replace damaged organs.

front:
**True or False?**

3D printed blood vessels are made from permanent synthetic materials.
back:
**False.**

3D printed blood vessels are made of **biodegradable materials**, and are used in surgery to replace damaged vessels.

front: 3D printed pills can be produced with precise <u>   </u> and drug combinations tailored to a patient.
back: 3D printed pills can be produced with precise **doses** and drug combinations tailored to a patient.

front: What is the potential benefit of tissue engineering for organ donation?
back: Tissue engineering has the **potential to reduce the need for organ donations**.

front: What benefit do 3D printed customised medicines offer?
back: They have the potential to **improve medication adherence and effectiveness**, because doses and combinations are tailored to the patient's needs.

front: Define **expert system**.
back: An expert system **mimics human knowledge and experience** and uses a combination of the two to **solve problems or answer questions**.

front: Name the five key characteristics of an expert system.
back: The five characteristics are the **knowledge base**, the **rule base**, the **inference engine**, the **interface** and the **explanation system**.

front: Define **knowledge base**.
back: The knowledge base is a **database of facts** used to generate rules that solve problems and make decisions.

front: Define **rule base**.
back: The rule base is a **set of rules or logic** used to apply the knowledge in the knowledge base to specific problems.

front: Define **inference engine**.
back: The inference engine is a program that **applies the rules in the rule base to the facts in the knowledge base** in order to solve problems.

front: What does the interface of an expert system do?
back: The interface provides a way for **users to interact with the system and provide input**.

front: What does the explanation system of an expert system do?
back: The explanation system provides the user with the **explanation and reasoning behind decisions or recommendations**, and gives a **percentage probability** of the accuracy of its conclusions.

front:
**True or False?**

The inference engine stores the facts that the expert system uses.
back:
**False.**

The **knowledge base** stores the facts. The **inference engine** applies the rules in the rule base to those facts to solve problems.

front: Give three examples of expert systems.
back: Examples include **equipment troubleshooting and repair**, **technical support** and **medical diagnosis systems**.

front: Give three advantages of an expert system.
back: Expert systems give **consistent results**, provide **faster responses**, **can store large amounts of data**, and are **unbiased**.

front: Give three disadvantages of an expert system.
back: An expert system is **only as good as the data entered**, its responses can be **cold and lack human emotion**, and it **requires training to use correctly**.

front: A medical expert system displays the probabilities of possible diagnoses and <u>  </u> .
back: A medical expert system displays the probabilities of possible diagnoses and **treatments**.

front: Define **POS**.
back: Point of Sale is a **computer terminal used to read product barcodes**.

front: What information does each product record contain in a stock control system?
back: Each product record contains its **price**, **stock level** and a **description**.

front: What happens when a barcode is matched with a record?
back: The information is **transferred to the POS terminal**, the **price is displayed on the screen**, and the **stock level is reduced by one**.

front: What triggers an automatic restocking process?
back: Restocking is triggered automatically when the **current stock level falls below the minimum reorder stock level**.

front: Define **EFTPOS**.
back: Electronic Funds Transfer at the Point of Sale is **how a payment is made to purchase goods or services using a card or an electronic device** such as a smartphone.

front: Name the three examples of EFTPOS.
back: The three examples are **chip and PIN**, **contactless**, and **near field communication (NFC)** devices.

front:
**True or False?**

Contactless payment requires the customer to enter a PIN.
back:
**False.**

**Contactless** allows faster transactions by **tapping the card on the terminal**. It is **chip and PIN** that requires the customer to enter a personal identification number.

front: Define **internet shopping**.
back: Internet shopping is the **act of purchasing goods or services online** through a website or mobile application.

front: Give three characteristics of internet shopping.
back: Online stores are **accessible through web browsers**, a **wide variety of products and services** is available, and stores are **convenient and often open 24/7**.

front: Give three advantages of internet shopping to the customer.
back: It is **time-saving and convenient**, offers **greater product variety** with access to the global market, allows **customisation options**, and brings **potential cost savings** from competitive pricing and online promotions.

front: Give three disadvantages of internet shopping to the customer.
back: There are **security concerns** including fraud and identity theft, **limited physical interaction** so products cannot be touched or tried, **delivery delays and fees**, and **impersonal customer service**.

front: Give three advantages of internet shopping to the business.
back: A business can **target prices and products at specific groups** using buying data, **update stock and prices more quickly** than a physical store, publicise offers **more cheaply than mail shots**, reach an **international customer base**, and gain **increased profits from lower overheads**.

front: Give three disadvantages of internet shopping to the business.
back: Businesses face **increased competition**, **digital fraud and security concerns**, **technical issues and downtime**, **costs of delivery and returns**, problems with **customer trust**, and **dependency on internet infrastructure**.

front: The automated stock system sends a signal to the <u>     </u> computer to order new items.
back: The automated stock system sends a signal to the **warehouse** computer to order new items.

front: Define **recognition system**.
back: A recognition system is a way of using **computer technology to automatically identify something**.

front: Give three common examples of recognition systems.
back: Common examples are **facial recognition**, **speech recognition** and **optical character recognition**.

front: Define **OMR**.
back: Optical Mark Recognition **detects marked areas on paper** by using a special machine to read the marks.

front: Give three examples of where OMR is used.
back: OMR is used for **multiple-choice examinations**, **barcodes** and **QR codes**, automating data collection and entry.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of OMR.
back: OMR gives **fast and efficient data collection** and **reduces manual entry errors**, but it is **limited to predetermined responses** and is **sensitive to poor marking or smudging**.

front: Define **OCR**.
back: Optical Character Recognition **converts printed or handwritten text into digital format**.

front: What is ANPR, and what type of system is it an example of?
back: Automated Number Plate Recognition is an example of **OCR**, used for reading number plates and controlling entry and exit at airport parking.

front: Give three disadvantages of ANPR.
back: There are **privacy concerns** because number plates are recorded, **number plates can be cloned**, **dirty or broken plates cannot be read**, and a **lack of staff could lead to vandalism**.

front: Define **RFID**.
back: Radio Frequency Identification Devices use **radio waves to identify and track objects**.

front: What are RFID tags made of, and what are the two types?
back: RFID tags are made of a **microchip and antenna**. They can be **passive**, using energy from the reader, or **active**, having their own power source.

front:
**True or False?**

A passive RFID tag has its own power source.
back:
**False.**

A **passive** tag uses **energy from the reader**. It is an **active** tag that has its own power source.

front: Why would active tags be used for livestock tracking on a farm?
back: **Active** tags would be used **because of the distance involved**, tracking each animal's location and medical data.

front: Define **NFC**.
back: Near field communication is a **subset of RFID** which allows communication between **two devices in very close proximity**.

front: Passports contain <u>    </u> chips, which are read by a reader to decrypt the data stored on them.
back: Passports contain **passive** chips, which are read by a reader to decrypt the data stored on them.

front: Define **GPS**.
back: The Global Positioning System is a satellite system **used to track the exact location of an object**.

front: How does GPS work?
back: GPS uses **orbiting satellites to receive, amplify and transmit signals**, with **radio frequencies** used to communicate between satellites and ground stations. It **requires a direct line of sight**.

front: How does a sat nav in a car calculate and display position?
back: The car's position is calculated using **GPS software**, data is **transmitted every few seconds**, an **algorithm calculates the speed and location**, and the **map is updated every few seconds**.

front: Give three advantages of satellite systems.
back: They offer a **wide coverage area**, **real-time data transmission**, **improved communication in remote locations**, and **accurate location tracking**.

front: Give three disadvantages of satellite systems.
back: They have **expensive setup and maintenance**, suffer **signal interference from weather or obstacles**, have **limited bandwidth and capacity**, and raise **privacy concerns and the potential for surveillance**.

front: Define **GIS**.
back: A geographic information system is a computer system that acts as a **database for geographic data**, storing any data that contains a **location component**.

front: Give the three categories of data a GIS can store.
back: A GIS stores **physical features** such as rivers, mountains and roads; **man-made** data such as buildings and utilities; and **social and economic** data such as demographics, crime rates and property value.

front: What are the two main features of a GIS?
back: A GIS can **analyse geographic data** to find patterns, trends and relationships, and **visualise geographic data using maps** to make it easier to understand.

front: Give three examples of where a GIS may be used.
back: A GIS can **assign the closest emergency services** to an emergency, help businesses **analyse customer demographics, competitors and gaps in the market**, and support **tracking deforestation, monitoring pollution and mapping wildlife habitats**.

front: Give three disadvantages of a GIS.
back: A GIS has a high **cost**, is **only as good as the data it uses**, needs **specialised training** to interpret the visual elements properly, and raises **data privacy concerns**.

front: Define **media communication**.
back: Media communication is a system of **creating, transmitting, storing and delivering media content** using a **global network of satellites**.

front: What three types of signal does media transmission include?
back: Media transmission includes **TV signals**, **radio signals** and **internet data**.

front:
**True or False?**

Satellite media communication is unaffected by the weather.
back:
**False.**

**Bad weather can affect the quality of the signal received**. Time delays can also cause audio and video sync issues, and satellites need regular monitoring and maintenance.

front: Media communication systems can act as <u>    </u>, bouncing signals over a large distance.
