back: Media communication systems can act as **relays**, bouncing signals over a large distance.

front: Define the **system life cycle**.
back: The system life cycle is a **structured process** that guides the **planning**, **creation**, **testing** and **deployment** of an information system.

front: What is the purpose of the analysis stage?
back: The purpose of the analysis stage is to gather detailed **requirements** from stakeholders and analyse them to understand **what the system should accomplish**.

front: Name the four research methods a systems analyst can use.
back: The four research methods are **observation**, **questionnaires**, **interviews** and **looking at the existing system**, including its paperwork.

front: Define **observation** as a research method.
back: Observation is watching users **interact with the current system** to see how it acts and works.

front: Give one disadvantage of observation.
back: People **do not always behave in the same way** when they are under observation.

front: Which research method allows the analyst to change questions based on the answers given?
back: **Interviews** allow the analyst to change questions based on responses, because they are one-to-one question and answer sessions.

front:
**True or False?**

Interviews allow employees to remain anonymous.
back:
**False.**

Interviews **cannot remain anonymous**, so employees may not give honest responses for fear of repercussions. **Questionnaires** can be anonymous.

front:
**True or False?**

Questionnaires are quick and inexpensive to use.
back:
**True.**

Questionnaires are **quick**, **inexpensive** and can be **anonymous**, but the analyst cannot ask follow-up questions and the response rate can be low.

front: Give one advantage of looking at the existing system.
back: Looking at the existing system lets the analyst **obtain information that cannot be obtained from other methods**.

front: Which six key aspects must be identified when analysing the current system?
back: The six key aspects are **inputs**, **outputs**, **processing**, **problems**, **user requirements** and **information requirements**.

front: Define **user requirements**.
back: User requirements are **what users need from the new system**.

front: What are data flow diagrams (DFDs) used for?
back: Data flow diagrams (DFDs) help analysts to understand the **inputs**, **outputs** and **processing** in the existing system.

front: A <u>**            **</u> is drawn up from the results of the analysis.
back: A **requirements specification** is drawn up from the results of the analysis.

front: What is the purpose of the design stage?
back: The purpose of the design stage is to develop architectural **blueprints for the system**, including **database design**, **user interfaces** and **system interfaces**.

front: What four things are defined when designing a file structure?
back: A file structure defines **field names**, **field lengths**, **data types** and **primary keys**.

front: What is a file made up of?
back: A file consists of **records**, and records are made up of **fields**.

front: Define **primary key**.
back: A primary key is the field that **uniquely identifies each record**.

front: Which data type stores data in a Yes/No or True/False format?
back: The **Boolean** data type stores data in a Yes/No or True/False format.

front: Which data type would be used for a postcode or a product code?
back: The **alphanumeric** data type would be used, because it stores a combination of **characters and numeric data**.

front:
**True or False?**

The character data type stores a single letter or symbol.
back:
**True.**

The **character** data type stores a **single letter or symbol**, such as A, B or C.

front: Define **validation routine**.
back: A validation routine is a **check placed on data being entered** to ensure it matches the design of the system.

front: Name the six validation routines.
back: The six validation routines are the **range check**, **length check**, **type check**, **format check**, **presence check** and **check digit**.

front: Which validation routine checks that a field has not been left blank?
back: A **presence check** looks to see if any data has been entered in a field.

front: Which validation routine would check a date of birth is entered as DD/MM/YY?
back: A **format check** ensures that data has been entered in the **correct format**.

front: Define **check digit**.
back: A check digit is a **numerical value** that is the **final digit of a larger code**, such as a barcode.

front: Validation routines prevent errors and maintain data <u>**        **</u>.
back: Validation routines prevent errors and maintain data **integrity**.

front: What is a data capture form used for?
back: A data capture form is used to **collect data from a user in a structured format**.

front: Give two ways a data capture form should aid the collection of data.
back: A data capture form should have a **user-friendly layout**, provide **clear instructions**, use **appropriate question types** and use **validation routines**.

front: What is the purpose of the testing stage?
back: The purpose of testing is to verify that the system **meets all requirements**, **functions correctly** and is **free of bugs**.

front: Define **test strategy**.
back: A test strategy is a **method of testing a completed system** to ensure **all parts work as intended**.

front: How is a system that is designed in modules tested?
back: Each module is tested **independently**, and testing is done again once all modules are **joined together**.

front:
**True or False?**

Once changes have been made to a system, it does not need to be tested again.
back:
**False.**

Testing is **repeated** once all changes have been made.

front: Name the five things a test design covers.
back: A test design covers **data structures**, **file structures**, **input formats**, **output formats** and **validation routines**.

front: Why are validation routines tested?
back: Validation routines are tested to check that the system **rejects unreasonable data** being inputted.

front: What four things does a test plan include?
back: A test plan includes the **test data**, the **expected outcomes**, the **actual outcomes** and any **remedial action**.

front: Define **remedial action**.
back: Remedial action is the **steps taken to fix identified issues**.

front: Name the four categories of test data.
back: The four categories of test data are **normal**, **extreme**, **abnormal** and **live**.

front: Define **normal data**.
back: Normal data is data that **should be accepted** by the system and that has a **known outcome**.

front: Define **extreme data**.
back: Extreme data is data that is **on the limits of what is acceptable**.

front:
**True or False?**

Extreme data should be rejected by the system.
back:
**False.**

Extreme data is **on the limits of what is acceptable**, so it is accepted. It is **abnormal data**, which is outside the limits of what is acceptable, that should be rejected.

front: <u>**      **</u> data is data from the old system used on the new system.
back: **Live** data is data from the old system used on the new system.

front: Why is live data useful when testing a new system?
back: Live data has **known outcomes**, so the results can be **compared** with the old system to ensure the new system works.

front: What is the purpose of the implementation stage?
back: The purpose of implementation is to **deploy the system to the production environment** and ensure all components work together in the **live setting**.

front: When does system implementation take place?
back: Implementation takes place **after a system has been fully tested** and is working correctly.

front: What are the two stages of system implementation?
back: The two stages are **transferring data from the old system to the new system** and the **system changeover**.

front: Define **changeover**.
back: A changeover is **moving from the old system to the new system**.

front: Name the four methods of changeover.
back: The four methods of changeover are **direct**, **parallel**, **pilot running** and **phased**.

front: Define **direct changeover**.
back: In a direct changeover the **old system is replaced by the new system immediately**.

front: Define **parallel running**.
back: In parallel running **both the old and the new systems run simultaneously** for a period before the old system is phased out.

front: Which changeover method implements the new system in one branch of a company?
back: **Pilot running** implements the new system in a **small, controlled environment** before full-scale implementation.

front: In <u>**      **</u> implementation the new system is introduced in stages, with each stage replacing a part of the old system.
back: In **phased** implementation the new system is introduced in stages, with each stage replacing a part of the old system.

front: Give one advantage of a direct changeover.
back: A direct changeover gives **fast implementation** and is **cost-effective**, because only one system is in operation.

front: Give two disadvantages of a direct changeover.
back: A direct changeover has a **high risk of failure**, **no fallback**, **no backup of the system**, and users **cannot be trained** on the new system beforehand.

front:
**True or False?**

Parallel running is cheaper than a direct changeover.
back:
**False.**

Parallel running is **time-consuming and resource-intensive** because two systems run at once. A **direct** changeover is the cost-effective method.

front: Give one advantage of parallel running.
back: Parallel running has a **lower risk** and allows **easy comparison** of the two systems.

front: Give one disadvantage of pilot running.
back: Pilot running gives **slower implementation**, **potential inconsistencies**, **confusion** because two systems are in use, and **no backup** for the branch using the new system.

front:
**True or False?**

Phased implementation reduces risk and is easier to manage.
back:
**True.**

Phased implementation gives **reduced risk** and is **easier to manage**, but it **takes longer** and there may be **compatibility issues**.

front: Define **technical documentation**.
back: Technical documentation is **detailed information on the system's inner workings and programming** for **developers and IT staff**.

front: What three things does technical documentation allow the system to be?
back: Technical documentation enables the system to be **maintained**, **repaired** and **updated**.

front: Define **user documentation**.
back: User documentation is **instructions and guidance for end-users on how to operate the system**.

front: What does user documentation enable end-users to do?
back: User documentation enables end-users to **effectively use the system** and **overcome problems**.

front: Name three items found in technical documentation but not in user documentation.
back: Items found only in technical documentation include the **program listing**, **program language**, **program flowcharts/algorithms**, **system flowcharts**, **file structures**, **list of variables**, **test runs** and **validation routines**.

front: Name three items found in both technical and user documentation.
back: Both include the **purpose of the system**, its **limitations**, the **hardware and software requirements**, the **input format**, the **output format** and **sample runs**.

front:
**True or False?**

A glossary of terms is part of technical documentation.
back:
**False.**

A **glossary of terms** is part of **user documentation**, along with frequently asked questions and a troubleshooting guide.

front:
**True or False?**

The limitations of a system appear in both technical and user documentation.
back:
**True.**

**Limitations**, meaning the known constraints or issues with the system, appear in **both** types of documentation.

front: Which two items in user documentation help a user solve common problems?
back: A **troubleshooting guide/helpline** and **frequently asked questions** help a user solve common problems.

front: Which type of documentation explains error messages and error handling?
back: **User documentation** explains **error messages** and **error handling**.

front: Give two instructions about records that appear in user documentation.
back: User documentation explains **adding records** and **deleting or editing records**.

front: What are system flowcharts used to show?
back: System flowcharts are **visual representations of the interactions between system components**.

front: What three things must you assess to evaluate a system?
back: You must assess the **efficiency**, the **ease of use** and the **appropriateness** of the solution.

front: What can you do once a system has been successfully evaluated?
back: You can **identify limitations** and **propose improvements**.

front: A system's efficiency is evaluated in terms of which three things?
back: Efficiency is evaluated in terms of **resource usage**, **time** and **cost**.

front: Give one question you would ask when evaluating efficiency.
back: You would ask whether the system **operates quicker than the previous system**, whether it **reduces staff time**, or whether it **reduces staff costs**.

front: Define **ease of use** in an evaluation.
back: Ease of use is **how user-friendly and accessible the solution is** for its intended audience.

front: Give one question you would ask when evaluating ease of use.
back: You would ask whether all users can **complete their tasks easily** and whether staff can **understand how to use the system with minimal training**.

front: How is the appropriateness of a solution evaluated?
back: Appropriateness is evaluated by **comparing the implemented solution with the original task requirements** and judging **how well it meets the intended purpose**.

front:
**True or False?**

User feedback forms part of the evaluation of a system.
back:
**True.**

Users' responses to the results of testing give **insights into potential issues and improvements** and help determine **overall user satisfaction**.

front:
**True or False?**

Evaluating a system only means checking whether it works.
back:
**False.**

Evaluation assesses the **efficiency**, **ease of use** and **appropriateness** of the solution, not just whether it functions.

front: Name two evaluation strategies.
back: Evaluation strategies include **comparing the final solution with the user requirements**, **identifying limitations**, **identifying further improvements**, **analysing feedback from users** and **comparing test results from the new system with the old system**.

front: What should be summarised when reporting the testing process in an evaluation?
back: The summary should cover the **test data**, the **expected outcomes** and the **actual outcomes**.

front: Define **physical safety**.
back: Physical safety is **creating a safe environment when using technology**, considering dangers that could lead to **serious injury or loss of life**.

front: Name four physical safety risks of using computers.
back: The risks are **electrocution**, **fire hazards**, **equipment overheating**, **trailing cables** as a trip hazard, and **heavy equipment falling** and causing injury.

front: What causes electrocution when using computers?
back: Electrocution is caused by **spilling drinks near electrical equipment** and by **touching live cables**.

front: Give two ways to prevent electrocution.
back: **Keep liquids away** from electrical equipment, ensure cables are **properly insulated**, **turn off and unplug** equipment before cleaning, and use **circuit breakers or fuses**.

front: What two things cause fire hazards?
back: Fire hazards are caused by **sockets being overloaded** and by **equipment overheating**.

front: Give two ways to prevent a fire caused by overloaded sockets.
back: Use **surge protectors**, ensure there are **enough plug sockets**, do not **plug too many devices into the same socket**, and do not **leave devices plugged in and unattended**.

front:
**True or False?**

Covering the air vents on a device helps prevent it overheating.
back:
**False.**

Air vents must **never be covered**. Equipment should be **properly ventilated and not obstructed** to prevent overheating.

front: What causes a trip hazard?
back: A trip hazard is caused by **cables not being properly secured or organised**.

front: Give two ways to prevent trip hazards.
back: Use **cable ties or clips**, keep cables **away from walkways**, secure cables **under desks**, use **cable covers**, and use **wireless devices** to reduce cables.

front: How can the risk of heavy equipment falling be reduced?
back: Ensure equipment is **properly secured and stable**, keep it **away from edges**, and **regularly check** the stability of locations containing devices.

front: What does the Data Protection Act (DPA) do?
back: The Data Protection Act is a law that **protects personal data from being misused**.

front: Name the three exemptions from the Data Protection Act.
back: The exemptions are **domestic purposes**, **law enforcement** and **intelligence services processing**.

front: Define **personal data**.
back: Personal data is any **data that can be used to identify an individual**.

front: Define **sensitive data**.
back: Sensitive data is a **subset of personal data** that, **if disclosed, could lead to personal harm**, so it requires **stricter protection**.

front: Give three examples of personal data.
back: Personal data includes a person's **name**, **address**, **date of birth**, **gender**, **personal images**, **payment details** and **passwords**.

front: Give three examples of sensitive data.
back: Sensitive data includes **medical history**, **political views**, **ethnic or racial origin**, **criminal activities**, **trade union membership**, **sexual orientation** and **biometric data**.

front: Define **biometric data**.
back: Biometric data is **body measurements used to identify us uniquely**, such as **fingerprints** or **facial features**.

front:
**True or False?**

A photograph of a student in school uniform counts as personal data.
back:
**True.**

A personal image in school uniform can be used to **identify and locate** the individual, so it is personal data.

front: The third data protection principle states that personal data must be adequate, relevant and not <u>**        **</u>.
back: The third data protection principle states that personal data must be adequate, relevant and not **excessive**.

front:
**True or False?**

A company may pass your personal data to another company without your permission.
back:
**False.**

Personal data must be collected for **specified and lawful purposes**, and a company **cannot pass the data on without permission**.

front: What right do you have if a company holds data about you that is wrong or out of date?
back: You have the right to have it **corrected or deleted**, because personal data must be kept **accurate and up to date**.

front: What must a company do with personal data it no longer needs?
back: The company must **delete it**, because personal data **will not be kept for longer than is necessary**.

front: What can happen if personal data is inappropriately disclosed?
back: It can lead to **privacy breaches**, **identity theft** or **misuse of the information**. Data could be **sold to third party companies**, used to hold someone to **ransom**, or used to commit a **physical crime**.

front: Give two ways to stop personal data being inappropriately disclosed.
back: Use **privacy settings** and **strong passwords**, limit access to **authorised individuals**, **think before you post**, check a website's details about how it uses data, and only use a **secure, encrypted connection**.

front: Define **e-safety**.
back: E-safety is **knowing about and using the internet safely and responsibly**, and knowing how to **protect yourself from potential dangers and threats**.

front: Which four activities does e-safety apply to?
back: E-safety applies to using the **internet**, **email**, **social media** and **online gaming**.

front: Give three reasons why e-safety is needed.
back: E-safety **protects personal information**, **prevents cyberbullying**, **guards against online scams**, **protects your digital reputation**, **prevents exposure to inappropriate content** and **guards against malware and viruses**.

front: Why does your digital reputation matter?
back: Your online behaviour and interactions can have **long-term consequences** in your **personal and professional life**.

front: Give two pieces of advice for staying safe when using the internet.
back: Use **trusted websites** recommended by teachers or reputable sources, use **search engines with filters** that only allow age-appropriate websites, and **never reveal personal information**.

front: What are the dangers of opening or replying to emails from unknown people?
back: The dangers include **phishing** and **spam**, and attachments from unknown senders can be harmful.

front: What should you check before sending personal data or images by email?
back: Check that you **know who the email is for**, send only to **people you know**, and do not send **identifiable content** such as school photos.

front: Give three ways to stay safe when using social media.
back: Know how to **block and report** people, use **privacy settings**, only accept **friend requests from people you know**, **do not distribute inappropriate images or language**, **respect other people's personal data**, and do not post details that can be used to **locate you**.

front:
**True or False?**

It is safe to meet an online contact face to face as long as you go alone.
back:
**False.**

You should **not meet anyone you do not know**. If you do meet an online contact, **take an adult** and meet in a **public place**.

front:
**True or False?**

You should use your real name as your username when gaming online.
back:
**False.**

You should **not use real names as usernames** when playing games online.

front: Give two rules for staying safe when playing games online.
back: Do not use **real names as usernames**, **never share personal or financial details** with other players, and know how to **block and report players** for inappropriate messages.

front: E-safety supports overall well-being by keeping a healthy balance between online and <u>**        **</u> lives.
back: E-safety supports overall well-being by keeping a healthy balance between online and **offline** lives.

front: What should you do if something you see or read online worries you?
back: You should **tell someone about it** and **block** the person responsible.

front: Define **hacking**.
back: Hacking is gaining **unauthorised access** to computer systems or networks to gain control, steal information or cause damage.

front: Name three weaknesses a hacker looks for.
back: A hacker looks for **unpatched software**, **out-of-date anti-malware** and **weak passwords**.

front:
**True or False?**

The only consequence of hacking is financial loss.
back:
**False.**

Hacking can also cause **data breaches**, the **installation of malware**, **data loss** and **identity theft**.

front: Define **phishing**.
back: Phishing is a form of **social engineering** in which fraudulent, legitimate-looking **emails** are sent to a large number of addresses, claiming to be from a reputable company, to gain access to a user's details.

front: Give two ways an organisation can prevent phishing.
back: Phishing can be prevented by **anti-spam filters**, **training staff** to recognise fraudulent emails, and **user access levels** that stop staff opening file types such as **.exe** and **.bat** files.

front: Define **pharming**.
back: Pharming is when a user types a website address into a browser and is **redirected to a fake website** designed to trick them into entering sensitive information.

front:
**True or False?**

In a pharming attack the user is tricked into clicking a link in an email.
back:
**False.**

The user types the address themselves; the attacker alters **DNS settings** or the user's **browser settings** to redirect them to the fraudulent website.

front: What is the difference between smishing and vishing?
back: Smishing uses **SMS messages** and vishing uses **fraudulent phone calls**, but both are forms of phishing used to obtain personal information.

front: Give two ways to protect yourself from smishing and vishing.
back: Do not click links in **unsolicited text messages**, never share personal information over the phone unless **you initiated the call**, **verify the caller's identity** independently, and check the sender's number carefully for anything suspicious.

front: Define **malware**.
back: Malware is any **software created with malicious intent** to cause harm to a computer system.

front: What makes a computer virus different from other malware?
back: A computer virus can **replicate itself** on a user's computer, and contains code that causes unwanted and unexpected events.

front: How does a Trojan get onto a computer?
back: A Trojan **disguises itself as legitimate software** while containing malicious code in the background.

front: Define **spyware**.
back: Spyware is software that allows a person to **spy on a user's activities**, recording the screen and logging **keystrokes** to gain access to passwords.

front: Name the three main methods of card fraud.
back: The three main methods of card fraud are **shoulder surfing**, **card cloning** and **keylogging**.

front: Card cloning is the copying of data from a credit or debit card by scanning the <u>        </u> through a skimmer machine.
back: Card cloning is the copying of data from a credit or debit card by scanning the **magnetic strip** through a skimmer machine.

front: Define **keylogging**.
back: Keylogging is software installed to **detect and store keystrokes** from the keyboard and send the data back to the criminal.

front: How can data be held securely?
back: Data can be held securely by storing it in an **encrypted format** and ensuring **authentication** is used, so that only **trusted sources** can access it.

front: Name four ways of storing data securely.
back: Data can be stored securely using **biometrics**, a **digital certificate**, **SSL**, **encryption**, a **firewall**, **two-factor authentication**, and **usernames and passwords**.

front: Define **biometrics**.
back: Biometrics is a way of authenticating a user by their **unique human characteristics**.

front: Give three examples of biometrics.
back: Examples are **fingerprint scans**, **retina scans** and **facial recognition**.

front: Give two benefits of using biometrics.
back: Biometric data is **unique to the person** and **difficult to copy or forge**, it is **always with the person**, and it eliminates attacks such as **shoulder surfing** and **key-logging**.

front: Give two drawbacks of using biometrics.
back: Collecting biometric data can be **intrusive**, scans **may not be recognised**, retina and iris recognition is **expensive to install**, and **low light, hats or glasses** cause problems for facial recognition.

front: Define **digital certificate**.
back: A digital certificate is a **digital file used to prove who stores the public key**.

front: Name three things a digital certificate contains.
back: A digital certificate contains the **public key**, **subject information**, **issuer information**, a **validity period**, a **serial number**, the **signature algorithm** and the **digital signature**.

front: Who issues digital certificates?
back: Digital certificates are issued by **trusted companies**, known as **certificate authorities (CAs)**, to ensure they are real and safe.

front: Define **Secure Socket Layer (SSL)**.
back: SSL is a **security protocol** used to **encrypt data transmitted over the internet**, helping to prevent **eavesdropping** and other forms of **interception**.

front: How does SSL use a digital certificate?
back: SSL sends a **digital certificate to the user's browser**. The certificate contains the **public key**, which is used for **authentication**, and once it is authenticated the transaction begins.

front:
**True or False?**

A digital certificate and SSL are the same thing.
back:
**False.**

A digital certificate is the **file that proves who holds the public key**. SSL is the **security protocol** that encrypts the data and sends the certificate to the browser.

front: Define **encryption**.
back: Encryption is a method of converting **plain text into ciphered text**, using complex mathematical algorithms to scramble the text.

front: Asymmetric encryption is also known as private key, <u>**      **</u> key encryption.
back: Asymmetric encryption is also known as private key, **public** key encryption.

front:
**True or False?**

Encryption prevents attacks on a network from happening.
back:
**False.**

Encryption **does not prevent the attacks from occurring**, but it does stop the attacker from **gaining access to the information**.

front: Define **firewall**.
back: A firewall is a **barrier between a network and the internet** that prevents **unwanted traffic** entering by **filtering requests** to ensure they are legitimate.

front: What is the difference between a hardware and a software firewall?
back: A **hardware** firewall protects the **whole network**, while a **software** firewall protects **individual devices**, monitoring the data going to and from each computer.

front: Name two attacks a firewall helps to prevent.
back: A firewall helps prevent **hackers**, **malware**, **unauthorised access to a network** and **DoS/DDoS attacks**.

front: Define **two-factor authentication (2FA)**.
back: Two-factor authentication is a security measure that requires users to provide **two separate forms of identification** to verify their identity.

front:
**True or False?**

Entering two different passwords is two-factor authentication.
back:
**False.**

2FA combines something the user **knows**, such as a password, with something the user **has**, such as a code sent to a smartphone or an authenticator application.

front: What are the two stages of two-factor authentication?
back: First the user enters a **username and password or PIN**, then the user enters a **one-time unique PIN sent to their mobile device**.

front: Why are passwords stored as encrypted text in a database?
back: So that even with **unauthorised access to the database**, a hacker would **not be able to read the individual passwords** of users.

front: What makes a strong password?
back: A strong password uses a combination of **uppercase and lowercase letters**, **numbers** and **special characters**, and is **changed regularly**.

front: Give one disadvantage of using passwords.
back: Complex passwords are **harder to remember**, having **too many passwords** is difficult, and hackers can break most passwords using **brute force attacks**.

front: Which law covers copyright?
back: Copyright is covered by the **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act**.

front: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act protect?
back: It protects the **intellectual property** of an individual or a company.

front: What three actions does copyright make illegal without permission?
back: It is illegal to **copy**, **modify** or **distribute** software or other intellectual property without the relevant permission.

front:
**True or False?**

You must apply for copyright before your original work is protected.
back:
**False.**

If work is original, copyright is **automatically applied**.

front: How long does copyright last?
back: Copyright does not expire until **25 to 70 years from the death of the creator**, depending on the type of work.

front: Whose responsibility is it to take action if work has been copied?
back: It is the responsibility of the **individual whose work was copied** to take action under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.

front: Name three primary breaches of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
back: Primary breaches are **copying an original work**, **issuing a copy to the public**, **renting or lending a copy to the public**, **performing, showing or playing the work in public**, and **making an adaptation** of it.

front: Name two secondary breaches of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
back: Secondary breaches are **importing a copy**, **possessing or dealing with a copy**, **providing the means to make copies**, **permitting the use of premises** for making copies, and **providing equipment** for a performance of a copy.

front: Define **software piracy**.
back: Software piracy is the **illegal copying and distribution of software**.

front: Name three methods companies use to prevent software piracy.
back: Companies use a **product key or licence**, an **agreement of terms and conditions** before installation, and **holograms** on the packaging. Some older software would only run with the **CD-ROM or memory stick physically in the device**.

front: How does a hologram show that software is genuine?
back: Holograms are **too difficult and costly for pirates to implement**, so packaging without one is usually an **illegal copy**.

front: A product key is a unique string of letters and numbers supplied with the software to <u>**        **</u> it.
back: A product key is a unique string of letters and numbers supplied with the software to **activate** it.

front: What does a licence agreement tell the user?
back: A licence agreement informs the user **exactly how they are legally allowed to use the product**, and they must agree to the terms before installation can finish.

front:
**True or False?**

Downloading videos from a streaming service and sharing them breaches the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
back:
**True.**

The Act covers **videos and audio**, and sharing them **prevents the copyright owner from receiving an income**.

front: Define **email**.
back: Email is a method of **exchanging messages and files over the internet**.

front: What are the three main uses of email?
back: The main uses are **personal communication**, **professional correspondence** and **marketing**.

front: What three things do company email guidelines cover?
back: Guidelines cover the **purpose** of the email, the use of **acceptable language**, and email **security**, including anti-virus software.

front: Give two rules about acceptable language in emails.
back: Use a **professional tone** and include a **clear subject line**. Never use **offensive or obscene** language or images, **racist or violent content**, or send **illegal material**.

front:
**True or False?**

Writing an email entirely in capital letters is acceptable.
back:
**False.**

You should **not use all capitals**, because it implies **shouting**.

front: Define **netiquette**.
back: Netiquette, short for **internet etiquette**, is the need to **respect others online**, including respecting their opinions in forums, messages and emails.

front: How should an email inbox be protected?
back: An inbox should be protected by **strong passwords** that are **frequently changed**, with **spam filters** and **antivirus software** in place at all times.

front: Why might a company use an email group?
back: An email group allows **mass communication with a defined set of recipients**, is **easier** than sending multiple emails, and ensures **no one misses out** on key information.

front: Give one drawback of email groups.
back: **Spammers can use them** to target a large group of people with ease.

front: What is the difference between CC and BCC?
back: **Carbon copy (CC)** includes additional recipients who **can be seen** by everyone, while **blind carbon copy (BCC)** lets additional recipients view the email **without the other recipients knowing**.

front: What does forwarding an email do?
back: Forwarding sends an **existing email to a new recipient**.

front: <u>**          **</u> allow files to be sent along with an email message.
back: **Attachments** allow files to be sent along with an email message.

front: Define **spam**.
back: Spam is **unwanted or unsolicited junk mail** which is sent in **large numbers** to inboxes.

front: What is spam usually used for?
back: Spam is usually used for **advertising**, or for **phishing and spreading malware**.

front:
**True or False?**

A phishing email pretends to come from a reputable company or organisation.
back:
**True.**

Phishing emails **act as a reputable company or organisation** in order to get **personal details** such as usernames and passwords.

front: Give three ways to recognise a spam email.
back: Spam often has **spelling or grammatical errors**, uses **broken English**, does **not address you by name**, asks you to **click a link and enter your details**, and pressures you to **act immediately**.

front: Give two ways to prevent spam.
back: Use an **anti-spam filter**, **do not agree to marketing emails**, **do not reply** to spam, and never complete a form by **clicking a link in an email**. Visit the website of your own accord instead.

front: Define **the Internet**.
back: The Internet is a **network of networks** which allows users to **share and distribute information outside of an organisation** and to **send and receive emails**.

front: Define **blog**.
back: A blog, short for **web log**, is a **journal shared on the internet** by a writer, regularly updated and often written in an **informal or conversational style**.

front: In what order are blog posts usually presented?
back: Blog posts are usually presented in **reverse chronological order**.

front:
**True or False?**

Other internet users can change the content of a blog.
back:
**False.**

Other users **cannot change the content** of a blog. They can only **read it** and leave **comments**.

front: Define **forum**.
back: A forum is an **online discussion site** where people hold conversations in the form of **posted messages**.

front: What are the categories a forum is divided into called?
back: Forum categories are called **threads**.

front: What is the difference between a moderated and an unmoderated forum?
back: A **moderated** forum is under the control of an **administrator** who decides what can be posted, preventing inappropriate content. An **unmoderated** forum has **no one in charge** and relies on **voluntary action between users**.

front: Define **wiki**.
back: A wiki is a website or web application that **allows users to add or edit content**.

front: Give two features of a wiki.
back: A wiki **facilitates collaboration and knowledge sharing**, its posts are **not in chronological order**, its structure is determined by the **content or its users**, and **changes can be tracked and reverted**.

front: What is the main difference between a blog and a forum?
back: A blog is managed by an **individual or small group** and readers can only comment, while a forum is focused on **peer-to-peer interaction** between users.

front: What is a social network?
back: A social network is a **platform where users can connect with others and share content** such as text, images, videos and links.

front: What do privacy settings on a social network allow a user to do?
back: Privacy settings allow users to **control who can see their content**.

front: Define **Internet Service Provider (ISP)**.
back: An Internet Service Provider is a **company that provides access to the Internet** to users and businesses, by leasing the equipment and telecommunication lines required.

front: What is a web browser?
back: A web browser is a **software application used to locate, retrieve and display content** on the World Wide Web.

front: Name three features of a web browser.
back: Most web browsers have a **home page**, the ability to **bookmark favourites**, a **history of visited websites**, and **hyperlinks** for navigating between pages.

front: Define **hyperlink**.
back: A hyperlink is a **word, phrase or image which references data** that the reader can follow by **clicking or tapping**, usually taking them to another web page.

front: Why are URLs used instead of IP addresses?
back: Websites are stored as **IP addresses**, which are **not user friendly**, so an **alphanumeric** web address is used for the benefit of humans.

front: What are the three stages a search engine works in?
back: A search engine works by **crawling**, **indexing** and **ranking**.

front: <u>**        **</u> is how websites are categorised based on their content, keywords and metadata.
back: **Indexing** is how websites are categorised based on their content, keywords and metadata.

front: Give two ways to refine a search.
back: Use **quotation marks** for exact phrases, **plus signs** for mandatory terms, and **minus signs** to exclude terms.

front: How do you judge whether information found online is reliable?
back: Consider the **reputation and credibility of the source**, check it against **other reputable sources**, consider whether it is **biased**, and check **how up to date** it is.

front: Give one argument for and one argument against policing the internet.
back: **For:** the internet contains **inappropriate and criminal material** that can harm younger and vulnerable users. **Against:** it goes against **freedom of speech**, and it is **not up to one person** to define what people find offensive.

front: Define **protocol**.
back: A protocol is a **set of rules that govern communication on a network**.

front: Name three internet protocols.
back: Internet protocols include **HTTP and HTTPS**, **FTP**, **SSL and TLS**, **VoIP** and **SMTP**.

front: What does HTTP stand for and what does it do?
back: HTTP stands for **Hypertext Transfer Protocol**. It allows **communication between clients and servers for website viewing**.

front: Give two things HTTP allows a client to do.
back: HTTP allows a client to **receive data** from the server, such as fetching a webpage, and to **send data** to the server, such as submitting a form or uploading a file.

front: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
back: HTTPS works in the same way as HTTP but with an **added layer of security**, because all data sent and received is **encrypted**.

front: What is HTTPS used to protect?
back: HTTPS is used to protect **sensitive information** such as **passwords**, **financial information** and **personal data**.

front: Define **File Transfer Protocol (FTP)**.
back: FTP is a protocol that allows **sending and receiving files between computers**.

front:
**True or False?**

FTP is the protocol used to display web pages in a browser.
back:
**False.**

**HTTP** displays web pages. **FTP** sends and receives **files** between computers, such as uploading files to a web server.

front: Give two advantages of FTP.
back: FTP offers **greater efficiency**, **support for bulk transfers and large files**, and the ability to **resume interrupted transfers**.

front: What is an FTP client?
back: An FTP client is a **software application that uses the FTP protocol** to make transferring files easier for users.

front: What is TLS?
back: TLS is the **successor to SSL**, and is also a **security protocol** used to provide secure communication over the internet.

front: What type of encryption do SSL and TLS use?
back: They use a combination of **symmetric and asymmetric encryption** to secure data and ensure **data integrity**.

front: SSL operates by encrypting a user's data using a <u>**      **</u> key.
back: SSL operates by encrypting a user's data using a **public** key.

front: Give three situations where SSL is used.
back: SSL is used for **online banking**, **online shopping**, **cloud storage**, **messaging**, **social networking websites** and **intranets and extranets**.

front: Define **file format**.
back: A file format is the **file type used to store the data in a file**. It defines the **structure and organisation** of the data and determines **which software can read** it.

front: Define **generic file format**.
back: A generic file format is a file type that is **compatible and allows sharing between different devices and software programs**.

front: What is a non-generic file?
back: A non-generic file is a file type that requires **special software or hardware** to be accessed.

front: Give two reasons why generic file types are needed.
back: They allow the **exchange of data across different applications**, they are **widely adopted** so many users and devices can access them, and they can be **created, edited and accessed across many different devices**.

front:
**True or False?**

JPEG images use lossy compression.
back:
**True.**

**JPEG** uses **lossy** compression, which significantly reduces file size while maintaining acceptable image quality.

front: Which two image file formats use lossless compression?
back: **PNG** and **GIF** both use lossless compression.

front: Why is PNG useful for logos and icons?
back: PNG has **transparency support**, so graphics can be placed onto different backgrounds easily, and it preserves **high-quality images** with small file sizes.

front: What is a GIF used for?
back: A GIF is used for **short, animated images** and **simple graphics**, keeping high image quality with small file sizes.

front: What is an MP4 file?
back: MP4 is a **multimedia container** rather than a single file format, and can be used for **video, image and audio**.

front: What is a MOV file?
back: MOV is a **multimedia container format developed by Apple**, used for storing **video, audio and other media data**.

front: What is the difference between MP3 and WAV?
back: **MP3** allows a **significant reduction in file size** with minimal difference in sound quality, while **WAV** is **uncompressed** and preserves the **original audio waveform**.

front: What is the difference between a .txt and an .rtf file?
back: A **.txt** file stores **plain, human-readable text** with no formatting, while an **.rtf** file stores **formatted text** with different styles, fonts, colours and images. A .txt file takes up **less memory**.

front: Define **comma separated values (.csv)**.
back: A CSV is a **plain text file format** used for storing data in a **structured manner**, in **rows and columns** with each cell **separated by a comma**.

front: Give two features of a PDF file.
back: A PDF **retains the layout and formatting** of a document across platforms, can be **password-protected** to stop unauthorised editing, and supports a **digital signature**.

front: What is the difference between a .zip and a .rar file?
back: Both are **compression containers**, but **.rar** uses a **proprietary compression algorithm** that generally gives **higher compression ratios**.

front: What does a .zip file allow you to do?
back: A .zip file allows **multiple files and folders to be compressed into a single, smaller archive**, using **lossless** compression algorithms.

front: What is HTML used for?
back: HTML is used for **creating and structuring web pages**. It contains **text-based code** that defines the structure, layout and content, and is **rendered by web browsers**.

front: A <u>**      **</u> file is attached to an HTML document and determines presentation and styling, such as colours, fonts and layout.
back: A **CSS** file is attached to an HTML document and determines presentation and styling, such as colours, fonts and layout.

front: Define **compression**.
back: Compression is **reducing the size of a file** so that it can be **transmitted** or **stored in secondary storage**.

front: Give two reasons why compression is needed.
back: Compression **maximises the amount of data** you can store on a device and **minimises the transfer time** of data being uploaded, downloaded or streamed across a network.

front: Other than compression, how can the file size of an image be reduced?
back: The file size of an image can be reduced by **reducing the colour depth** or the **resolution**.

front: What are the two methods of compression?
back: The two methods of compression are **lossy** and **lossless**.

front: Define **lossy compression**.
back: Lossy compression is when **data is lost** in order to reduce the size of a file on secondary storage. It is **irreversible**.

front: Define **lossless compression**.
back: Lossless compression is when **data is encoded** in order to reduce the size of a file on secondary storage. It is **reversible**, so the file can be **returned to its original state**.

front: What is the key difference between lossy and lossless compression?
back: Lossy is **irreversible** because **data is lost**, while lossless is **reversible** because **data is encoded** and the file can be returned to its original state.

front:
**True or False?**

Lossless compression loses less data than lossy compression.
back:
**False.**

Lossless compression **does not lose any data**. It **encodes** the data so the file can be returned to its **original state**, while lossy compression **permanently removes** data.

front:
**True or False?**

Lossless compression reduces file size as dramatically as lossy compression.
back:
**False.**

Lossless compression reduces the size of a file, but **not as dramatically as lossy** compression.

front: When is lossy compression suitable?
back: Lossy is only suitable for data where **reducing quality is acceptable**, for example **images, video and sound**.

front: When is lossless compression suitable?
back: Lossless is more suitable for data where a **loss in quality is unacceptable**, for example **documents**.

front: Give three file types that use lossy compression.
back: **JPEG** images, **MP3** audio and **MPEG-4** video all use lossy compression.

front: Give three file types that use lossless compression.
back: **PNG** images, **ZIP** files and **RAR** files all use lossless compression.

front: How does lossless compression work on a document?
back: Algorithms analyse the contents looking for **patterns and repetition**. Repeating characters are replaced with a single character and the number of occurrences, so 'EEEEE' becomes **'E5'**.

front: How does lossy compression reduce the size of a photograph?
back: It **groups similar colours together**, reducing the number of colours in the image without compromising the overall quality.

front: Define **audience**.
back: The audience is the **specific group of users that will be using the ICT solution**.

front: Define **purpose**.
back: The purpose is **why the ICT solution was created**.

front: What two things must you understand before designing an ICT solution?
back: You must understand the **audience characteristics** and the **needs of the audience**.

front: Name the five characteristics of an audience.
back: The five characteristics are **age**, **location**, **education and technical skill**, **interests** and **accessibility needs**.

front: How does the age of an audience affect a design?
back: **Younger** audiences are generally **open to new interfaces**, while **older** audiences may prefer a more **intuitive design** and **require training**.

front: What three things does the location of an audience affect?
back: Location affects **cultural references**, **access to high speed internet** and **language**.

front: What does the education and technical skill of an audience determine?
back: It determines the **level of complexity** the audience can handle.

front: Why should an audience's interests be considered?
back: Interests **influence design elements and the user experience**, so the solution can be made to **cater to what users enjoy**.

front: Which three accessibility needs should a solution consider?
back: A solution should consider users with **visual impairments**, users with **hearing impairments**, and users with **limited mobility**.

front: Give three accessibility features an ICT solution could include.
back: Accessibility features include **screen readers**, **high contrast mode**, **closed captions**, **transcripts** and **alternative control methods** such as voice commands.

front:
**True or False?**

Every audience should be given the same interface, whatever their age or skill level.
back:
**False.**

The design must match the **audience characteristics**, because age, education and technical skill change the **level of complexity** users can handle.

front: What two options are offered when creating a new document?
back: You can select a **blank document** or choose from a **bank of templates**.

front: Name three editing techniques for text and numbers.
back: Editing techniques include **highlight**, **delete**, **move**, **cut**, **copy**, **paste** and **drag and drop**.

front: What is the difference between cut and copy?
back: **Cut** removes the selection from its original location, while **copy** makes a **duplicate**. **Paste** then inserts the cut or copied material.

front: Define **drag and drop**.
back: Drag and drop is **clicking on the selected material**, holding the mouse button down, **moving the cursor to the desired location** and then releasing the button.

front: What does highlighting text allow you to do?
back: Highlighting uses the mouse to **select the text or numbers you want to manipulate**.

front: Name four objects that can be placed into a document.
back: Objects include **text**, **images**, **screenshots**, **shapes**, **tables**, **graphs or charts**, **spreadsheet extracts** and **database extracts**.

front: What two things can be adjusted about an object placed in a document?
back: You can adjust its **size** and its **position** in the document.

front: Name the four text wrapping options.
back: The four options are **above**, **below**, **square** and **tight**.

front: What is 'tight' text wrapping?
back: With tight wrapping the text **closely wraps around the object, following its shape**.

front:
**True or False?**

'Square' text wrapping follows the exact shape of the object.
back:
**False.**

**Square** wrapping forms a **square around the object**. It is **tight** wrapping that follows the object's shape.

front: Name three ways the layout of a page can be changed.
back: Page layout can be changed by altering the **size**, the **orientation** and the **number of columns**.

front: Define **gutter margin**.
back: A gutter margin provides **extra space on either side of a document** so that text is **not obscured by a binding mechanism** when the document is folded or opened.

front: What happens if a document has no gutter margin?
back: Printed information **can be hidden or difficult to read** where the document is bound.

front: Give two benefits of using a gutter margin.
back: A gutter margin gives **improved readability** and **enhanced aesthetics**.

front: Define **pagination**.
back: Pagination is a method of **dividing information into manageable chunks** to control the **layout and organisation** of a document.

front: Where is pagination used?
back: Pagination is used in **printed materials** and in **websites and applications**.

front: What does a page break do?
back: A page break forces content to **start on a new page even when there is still space available**.

front: Give two common uses of a page break.
back: Page breaks are used to start a **new chapter or section**, to **separate graphics and tables** from surrounding text, and to ensure page elements **appear at the top of a page**.

front: What does a column break do?
back: A column break **divides a page into multiple columns** to suit specific content types.

front: Give one common use of a column break.
back: Column breaks are used to create a **newsletter or brochure** and to **format content for easier viewing on screen**.

front: What does a section break do?
back: A section break creates **independent sections that can be formatted differently**.

front:
**True or False?**

A section break allows the page orientation to be changed for one part of a document.
back:
**True.**

A section break creates independent sections, so **page orientation** and **column layouts** can differ within the same document.

front: Formatting should always meet the needs of the <u>**        **</u> and purpose.
back: Formatting should always meet the needs of the **audience** and purpose.

front: What does formatting text mean?
back: Formatting text is **changing the visual appearance of text** in a document.

front: Name three common text formatting options.
back: Common text formatting includes **fonts**, **colours**, **case**, **emphasis**, and **subscript and superscript**.

front: Define **tabulation**.
back: Tabulation is **setting text to be indented at specific points**.

front: How can line spacing be changed?
back: Line spacing is altered from the **Home tab**, using the **'Line and Paragraph Spacing'** button or by opening the **paragraph settings**.

front: What two types of list can be created in a document?
back: You can create **bulleted** and **numbered** lists.

front: What does the find and replace tool do?
back: It changes **all instances of a word or phrase automatically**.

front: What two things can be matched when finding words in a document?
back: You can match the **case** and match **whole words**.

front: Define **hyperlink** in a document.
back: A hyperlink is an **electronic shortcut** to a **section in a document**, to **other documents** or to **websites**.

front: What can a hyperlink be added to?
back: A hyperlink can be added to **text or objects**.

front: Define **bookmark**.
back: A bookmark **flags a specific area within a document**.

front:
**True or False?**

A bookmark can be clicked to jump to a place in a document.
back:
**False.**

Bookmarks are **not clickable**. A **hyperlink** can be used to navigate to them.

front: Define **header**.
back: A header is the area at the **top of a document** that can be used to **help identify** it.

front: Define **footer**.
back: A footer is the area at the **bottom of a document** that can be used to **help identify** it.

front: Name three things a header or footer can contain.
back: A header or footer can contain the **document name**, the **author** and the **company logo**.

front: Give two benefits of using headers and footers.
back: They **save time**, because they only need to be added once and are replicated on each page, and they **reduce the chance of data errors**.

front: Name three automated objects used in headers and footers.
back: Automated objects include the **date and time**, **page numbering** and the **total number of pages**.

front: Why are automated objects used in headers and footers?
back: They **enhance the professionalism** of a document.

front: How can the contents of a header or footer be aligned?
back: They can be aligned to the **left margin**, the **right margin**, or **centred within the margins**.

front: Define **house style**.
back: A house style is when a business **consistently applies visual design elements across different media** to make them **recognisable**. It is a set of guidelines that ensures a consistent **brand identity**.

front: Name four design elements included in a house style.
back: A house style includes the **logo**, the **colours**, the **writing style and fonts**, and the **layout**.

front: Name three places a house style can be used.
back: A house style can be used on **letterheads**, **websites**, **posters**, **presentations** and **advertising**.

front: How does a house style help customers?
back: It makes the company's documents and products **instantly identifiable** to clients or customers.

front: Give two ways a house style streamlines the creation of documents.
back: It **reduces the time and cost** spent setting up and formatting documents, and it **reduces the risk of errors**.

front: How is a table created?
back: A table is created by **specifying the desired number of rows and columns**, using a **menu option**, by **typing them in**, or by **dragging the cursor** to the desired table size.

front: Name three ways a table can be edited.
back: You can **insert rows and columns**, **delete rows and columns**, and **merge cells**.

front: Define **merge cells**.
back: Merging cells **joins two or more cells into one**.

front: Why is a table formatted?
back: A table is formatted to improve **readability** and **visual appeal**.

front: Name three ways a table can be formatted.
back: You can set **horizontal cell alignment**, set **vertical cell alignment**, **show or hide cell borders**, **colour the background of a cell**, and **adjust the row height and column width**.

front: Which two features help a user navigate a document effectively?
back: **Bookmarks** and **hyperlinks** help a user navigate a document.

front: Define **bookmark**.
back: A bookmark **marks a place in a document** that the user wishes to be able to **find and navigate to again** easily.

front: Define **hyperlink**.
back: A hyperlink is a **clickable link** that can navigate to **another place in a document**, or to an **external webpage or file**.

front: What is the difference between a bookmark and a hyperlink?
back: A hyperlink is a **clickable link** that takes the user somewhere, while a bookmark simply **marks a place** in the document to return to.

front: How do you create a bookmark?
back: **Highlight the text** you wish to bookmark, then click **'Insert bookmark'**.

front: How do you delete a bookmark?
back: Click the **bookmarks button** and then select **'Delete'**.

front: How do you create a hyperlink?
back: **Highlight the text** you wish to link, then click **'Insert'** followed by **'Link'**.

front: How do you remove a hyperlink?
back: Highlight the linked text, click **'Insert'**, then **'Link'**, then **'Remove Link'**.

front:
**True or False?**

A hyperlink can only link to a place within the same document.
back:
**False.**

A hyperlink can navigate to another place in the document **or** to an **external webpage or external file**.

front: Define **image editing**.
back: Image editing is the process of **manipulating images and changing them to suit the user's end goal**.

front: Name four image editing techniques.
back: Techniques include **placing an image with precision**, **resizing**, **cropping**, **rotating**, **reflecting (flipping)**, **adjusting brightness and contrast**, and **grouping and layering**.

front: How can an image be placed with precision?
back: By **selecting the image and dragging it** to the desired location, or by using **coordinates or alignment tools** where the software allows.

front: What does maintaining the aspect ratio mean?
back: It means the image's **width and height change at the same rate**, which **prevents distortion**.

front:
**True or False?**

Adjusting the aspect ratio keeps the image's original proportions.
back:
**False.**

Adjusting the aspect ratio **changes the shape and proportions** of the image. Maintaining it is what prevents distortion.

front: Define **cropping**.
back: Cropping is **cutting out and discarding parts of an image**, keeping only the selected portion.

front: Rotating an image means turning it around a <u>**        **</u> point.
back: Rotating an image means turning it around a **central** point.

front: Which rotations are most commonly offered by software?
back: Software allows rotation to **any angle**, and commonly offers **90 degrees** and **180 degrees** as options.

front: Define **reflecting** an image.
back: Reflecting, or **flipping**, an image means creating a **mirror image of the original**.

front: In which two directions can an image be flipped?
back: An image can be flipped **horizontally**, from left to right, or **vertically**, from top to bottom.

front: What is the difference between brightness and contrast?
back: **Brightness** affects **all pixels equally**, making the image lighter or darker. **Contrast** adjusts the **difference between light and dark values**, making the image appear more or less detailed.

front:
**True or False?**

Adjusting brightness changes all pixels in the image equally.
back:
**True.**

**Brightness** affects all pixels in the image equally, making the whole image **lighter or darker**.

front: What is the difference between grouping and layering images?
back: **Grouping** combines images so they can be **moved or transformed as a single unit**, while **layering** places images **on top of each other**.

front: How can layered images be reordered?
back: The order can be changed by moving an image to the **front** or to the **back**.

front: Define **file compression**.
back: File compression is **reducing the size of a file** so that it **takes up less storage space** and makes **file transmission faster**.

front: Which element of a file is often the largest?
back: **Images** are often the largest element of a file.

front: What two ways can an image be resized or resampled to reduce file size?
back: By **reducing the resolution** and by **reducing the colour depth**.

front: Define **resolution**.
back: Resolution is the **total amount of pixels that make up an image**.

front: How is the resolution of an image calculated?
back: Resolution is calculated by **multiplying the height and width** of the image in pixels.

front: What is the effect of a higher resolution?
back: In general, the **higher the resolution the more detail** there is in the image, so the **higher the quality**.

front: How does reducing the resolution reduce file size?
back: Reducing the resolution **decreases the number of pixels**, which reduces the file size.

front: Define **colour depth**.
back: Colour depth is the **number of bits stored per pixel** in an image.

front: How does reducing the colour depth reduce file size?
back: Reducing the colour depth means **using fewer bits**, and therefore **fewer colours**, which reduces the file size.

front:
**True or False?**

Reducing resolution or colour depth has no effect on image quality.
back:
**False.**

Reducing either one can cause a **loss of image quality**, especially when the image is viewed at larger sizes.

front: Define **spell check software**.
back: Spell check software is **built into many word processing applications** and compares the **words typed in a document** with **those held in its dictionary**.

front: What happens to a word that does not match the dictionary?
back: It is **flagged and highlighted** for the user to check, most commonly by being **underlined in red**.

front: Give two examples of correctly spelt words that may still be flagged.
back: **Proper nouns** and **words in other languages** are often flagged even when spelt correctly.

front:
**True or False?**

A word flagged by a spell checker is always spelt incorrectly.
back:
**False.**

If a word is **not in the dictionary but is spelt correctly**, it will still be flagged. Proper nouns are a common example.

front: Why would the name of a specific beach be flagged by a spell checker?
back: It is a **proper noun**, so it is **not in the dictionary**. It can be **added to the dictionary** so that it is not flagged if used again.

front: Why should you use your own judgement with automated suggestions?
back: Automated suggestions **may not always be accurate or appropriate**, and the software may not recognise some **technical terms or jargon**.

front: What is the purpose of a validation check?
back: A validation check ensures data is **accurate, complete and meets specific criteria before it is processed**.

front: What two things does a validation check help to achieve?
back: It helps to **minimise data entry errors** and to **maintain the integrity of the data**.

front: Define **verification**.
back: Verification is a method of checking that data being **copied from one medium to another does not contain errors**.

front:
**True or False?**

Verification prevents all errors in data entry.
back:
**False.**

Verification **does not prevent all errors**. It **helps to reduce errors** in the data entry process.

front: Name the two most common verification techniques.
back: The two most common techniques are **visual verification** and **double data entry verification**.

front: Define **visual verification**.
back: Visual verification is a **manual method** of verifying data by **comparing the source with the entered data**.

front: Define **double data entry verification**.
back: Double data entry verification is a method where **data is entered twice and then compared for inconsistencies**.

front: What is the difference between verification and proofreading?
back: **Proofreading** is **checking the content of the data for errors**, while **verification** is **comparing the data with the original**.

front: What is the difference between verification and validation?
back: **Verification** ensures data has been **entered or copied correctly**, while **validation** makes sure the data is **sensible, reasonable and within acceptable boundaries**.

front:
**True or False?**

Validation checks that data is sensible, reasonable and within acceptable boundaries.
back:
**True.**

That is **validation**. **Verification** is the separate check that data has been copied correctly from the original.

front: Give one reason why data is verified on entry.
back: To ensure that the data entered has been **copied correctly**.

front: Why are both verification and validation needed?
back: Both are essential in maintaining **data accuracy and quality**.

front: Define **database**.
back: A database is a **structured, persistent collection of data** that allows easy **storage, retrieval and management** of information.

front: Give two benefits of an electronic database.
back: It is **easier to add, delete, modify and update data**, data can be **backed up and copied more easily**, and **multiple users from multiple locations** can access it at the same time.

front: Name the two main types of database.
back: The two main types are **flat file** and **relational**.

front: Define **flat file database**.
back: A flat file database stores **all data in a single table**.

front: Give two drawbacks of a flat file database.
back: A flat file causes **data redundancy**, uses **inefficient storage**, is **harder to maintain**, and risks **inconsistent data** if a repeated value is not changed everywhere.

front: Define **relational database**.
back: A relational database organises data into **multiple tables** and uses **keys to connect related data**.

front: Give two benefits of a relational database.
back: A relational database **reduces data redundancy**, makes **efficient use of storage** and is **easier to maintain**.

front: How does a relational database avoid inconsistent data?
back: Each piece of data is stored **only once**, so changing one piece of data updates it in the **entire database**.

front:
**True or False?**

A flat file database stores data in multiple linked tables.
back:
**False.**

A **flat file** database stores all data in a **single table**. It is a **relational** database that uses multiple linked tables.

front: Define **table** in a database.
back: A table is a **complete set of records about the same subject or topic** in a database.

front: Define **record**.
back: A record is a **complete set of fields on a single entity** in a table, shown as a **row**.

front: Why is repeating a tutor's name in every student row a problem?
back: It creates **redundant data**. If the tutor's name changed, **every instance** would need editing, and missing one would leave the table with **inconsistent data**.

front: Define **field**.
back: A field is a **single piece of data in a table**, shown as a **column**.

front: What is the difference between a field and a record?
back: A **field** is a single piece of data, shown as a **column**, while a **record** is a **group of related fields** representing one data entry, shown as a **row**.

front: Define **data type**.
back: A data type is the **type of data that can be held in a field**, and is defined when designing a table.

front: Name four common data types.
back: Common data types are **numeric** (whole or decimal), **character/string** for text data, **date/time**, and **Boolean** for true or false values.

front: Which data type would be used for the price of a car?
back: The **numeric** data type would be used for a price.

front:
**True or False?**

A Boolean field stores true or false values.
back:
**True.**

The **Boolean** data type stores **true or false** values.

front: Define **primary key**.
back: A primary key is a **unique field that can be used to identify a record in a table**.

front: Define **foreign key**.
back: A foreign key is a **field in a table that refers to the primary key in another table**.

front: What is a foreign key used for?
back: A foreign key is used to **link tables** and **create relationships** between them.

front:
**True or False?**

The same primary key value can appear on more than one record in a table.
back:
**False.**

A primary key is a **unique** field, so each record has its **own** primary key value.

front: An orders table contains a customer_id field. Which type of key is it?
back: It is a **foreign key**, because it refers to the **primary key** in the customers table and links an order back to the customer who made it.

front: State one benefit of using a relational database.
back: A relational database **reduces data redundancy** and **reduces data inconsistency**.

front: What two things can be used to perform calculations in a database?
back: Calculations use **arithmetic operations** or **numeric functions**.

front: Define **calculated field**.
back: A calculated field is a field that **carries out a calculation based on other number fields** in the database.

front: Give an example of a calculated field.
back: A `stockvalue` field could calculate `unit_price` multiplied by `stock`, which **multiplies the price of each item by its quantity** to find the **total value of the stock**.

front: Define **calculated control**.
back: A calculated control is an **object placed on a form or report** to display the **result of an expression**.

front: What happens to the result shown by a calculated control?
back: The result is **displayed on the form** but is **not stored in the database**.

front: Name the four basic arithmetic operations available in a database.
back: The four operations are **addition**, **subtraction**, **multiplication** and **division**.

front:
**True or False?**

`FinalCost = TotalCost - Discount` is an example of a subtraction operation.
back:
**True.**

Subtracting a discount field from the total cost is a **subtraction** operation performed at run time.

front: What are aggregate functions used for?
back: Aggregate functions **calculate statistical information about a set of records**.

front: Name the five aggregate functions.
back: The five aggregate functions are **SUM**, **AVERAGE**, **MAX**, **MIN** and **COUNT**.

front: Which aggregate function finds the highest number in a column?
back: **MAX** finds the highest number in a column, and **MIN** finds the lowest.

front: The SUM function adds together all the numbers in a <u>**      **</u>.
back: The SUM function adds together all the numbers in a **column**.

front: Define **sorting**.
back: Sorting is a database function that helps **organise and present data in a meaningful way**.

front: What is the difference between ascending and descending order?
back: **Ascending** sorts data from **smallest to largest**, such as A to Z or 1 to 100. **Descending** sorts from **largest to smallest**, such as Z to A or 100 to 1.

front: Give an example of sorting on a single criterion.
back: Sorting a list of customers into **ascending order by their last names** uses a single criterion.

front: Give an example of sorting on multiple criteria.
back: Sorting customers **first by last name** in ascending order, and then **by city** in descending order within each last name, uses multiple criteria.

front: Define **searching**.
back: Searching is the process of using **keywords, phrases or criteria** to **find specific information** within a database.

front: Searching in databases is typically done using <u>**        **</u>.
back: Searching in databases is typically done using **queries**.

front:
**True or False?**

A query can only be based on a single criterion.
back:
**False.**

Queries can be based on a **single criterion or multiple criteria**.

front: What is the difference between the AND and OR operators?
back: **AND** returns true if **both conditions are met**, while **OR** returns true if **at least one condition is met**.

front: What does the NOT operator return?
back: **NOT** returns true if the condition is **not met**.

front: What is the LIKE operator used for?
back: **LIKE** returns true if the value **matches a pattern**, and is used with **wildcards**.

front: Name three comparison operators.
back: The comparison operators are **>**, **<**, **=**, **>=**, **<=** and **<>**.

front: What do the wildcard characters %, _ and * represent?
back: **%** represents **zero, one or multiple characters**, **_** represents a **single character**, and **\*** represents **all**.

front: Define **database form**.
back: A form is a tool used to **capture data to be stored in a database**.

front: Give two examples of a form.
back: An **online form to sign up to a website**, and **filling in personal details on a mobile device to join a gym**.

front: Name the five characteristics of good form design.
back: Good form design has **simplicity**, **ease of use**, an **intuitive layout**, **clear labels** and **appropriate controls**.

front: What does an intuitive layout mean on a form?
back: **Related fields are grouped together** and the **sequence of fields follows a logical order**.

front: Why should each field on a form have a clear label?
back: A clear, concise label **indicates what information is expected** in that field.

front: Name three control elements used on a form.
back: Controls include **radio buttons**, **check boxes**, **drop-down menus**, a **submit button**, a **save button**, and **next and previous record buttons**.

front: When are radio buttons used?
back: Radio buttons are used when there is a list of **two or more options that are mutually exclusive**.

front: When are check boxes used?
back: Check boxes are used when the user can **select multiple options from a list**.

front: When are drop-down menus used?
back: Drop-down menus are used when you want to provide **many options but conserve space**.

front:
**True or False?**

Check boxes should be used when the options are mutually exclusive.
back:
**False.**

**Radio buttons** are used for mutually exclusive options. **Check boxes** are used when the user can select **multiple** options.

front: Why is white space important on a form?
back: White space **improves readability** and **reduces cognitive load**.

front: What should be considered about fonts on a data entry form?
back: Choose appropriate **font styles and sizes**, aiming for **consistency and readability**.

front: Define **spreadsheet**.
back: A spreadsheet is software used to **analyse**, **visualise** and **manipulate** data.

front: What three things is a spreadsheet made up of?
back: A spreadsheet is made up of **cells**, **rows** and **columns**.

front: What is a cell?
back: A cell is **one box** on the spreadsheet, referenced using its **cell reference**, such as A1.

front: What is the difference between a row and a column?
back: A **row goes across** and is referenced using the **number down the side**. A **column goes down** and is referenced using the **letter at the top**.

front:
**True or False?**
